Why: The foundation squat pattern. Builds the movement before load and is useful for warm ups, high rep BURN work and beginners. Band and pause variations add a twist: mini bands cue the knees out, pulses keep tension, dead stops kill the bounce.
Cue 1: Feet shoulder width, toes slightly out, tripod foot
Cue 2: Sit down between the hips, knees track over the toes
Cue 3: Stand tall and squeeze the glutes
Common faults: Heels lifting; Knees caving; Folding forward at the hips
Progress to: Goblet Squat (KB) (G2); Goblet Squat (DB) (G2); Barbell Box Squat (G2)
Progress by: Add a pause, tempo, then load (goblet squat)
Regress by: Squat to a box, TRX assisted squat
Same level swaps: Frog Squat; Prisoner Squat; Mini Band Squat
Joint notes: Generally joint friendly. Use a box with knee pain, heel elevation with stiff ankles.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 12 to 20 reps (or 30 to 40s)
Coach sources: Squat University, Paul Chek (Primal Pattern), Dan John

Why: Links a squat and an overhead press into one total body movement. Very metabolic, great for BURN and HYBRID sessions, and the legs help drive the weight overhead so people can press more.
Variation notes: Combination move: trains two qualities at once, efficient for HYBRID and BURN; keep technique of both parts clean before speeding up.
Cue 1: Squat with the weight in the rack
Cue 2: Drive up hard and use that momentum to press overhead
Cue 3: Lock out with biceps by the ears, ribs down, then lower back to the rack
Common faults: Pressing before the legs finish the drive; Arching the low back at the top; Losing the rack position and squatting with the elbows dropped
Progress to: Barbell Thruster (G4); Double KB Front Squat to Press (G4); Barbell Front Rack Squat to Press (G4)
Progress by: Add load, double KBs, barbell, more rounds or density
Regress to: DB Sumo Squat (G2); Goblet Squat (DB) (G2); DB Suitcase Squat (G2)
Regress by: Goblet squat to press, landmine squat to press, split into separate squat and press
Same level swaps: DB Thruster; DB Thrusters; KB Thruster
Joint notes: Needs pain free overhead range. With shoulder pain swap to squat to landmine press. Watch technique as fatigue builds in circuits.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 8 to 12 reps, or 30 to 40s in circuits

Muscles: Quads, glutes, upper back, shoulders, core
Why: The overhead squat exposes stiffness at the ankles, hips, T spine and shoulders all at once, which is why Squat University and the FMS use it as a screen. With a dowel it is an excellent mobility drill; loaded it is a high skill G4 lift.
Cue 1: Arms locked overhead, biceps by the ears, push up into the dowel or weight
Cue 2: Sit down between the hips with the chest proud
Cue 3: Keep the bar over the middle of the foot throughout
Common faults: Arms drifting forward; Lower back rounding at the bottom; Heels lifting
Progress to: Anderson Squat (G4); Tempo Back Squat (G4); Paused Back Squat (G4)
Progress by: Dowel → light DB/plate → barbell overhead squat
Regress to: DB Sumo Squat (G2); Goblet Squat (DB) (G2); DB Suitcase Squat (G2)

Same level swaps: Dowel Overhead Squat
Joint notes: Shoulder demanding: avoid loading with shoulder pain or impingement. Use a dowel as a warm up screen instead.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 5 to 8 reps, light, slow

Why: The box sets a consistent, safe depth and teaches people to sit back and control the descent. It is the best teaching squat for beginners and painful knees and, with a barbell or SSB, a classic DeFranco/Westside strength builder.
Cue 1: Box at a height where the spine stays neutral
Cue 2: Sit back and down with control, touch the box lightly (don't crash)
Cue 3: Stay braced, drive up through the whole foot
Common faults: Plonking down and relaxing on the box; Rocking back to get up; Knees caving as they stand
Progress to: Barbell Box Squat (G2); Banded Barbell Box Squat (G2)
Progress by: Lower the box, add load (goblet then SSB/barbell), pause on the box without relaxing, remove the box
Regress by: Raise the box, TRX assisted box squat, sit to stand
Same level swaps: Goblet Box Squat; Box Squat (High Box)
Joint notes: Excellent for knee pain and older members: adjust height to the pain free range. Lower the box as mobility and control improve.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Muscles: Lower and middle traps, rear shoulders, rotator cuff
Why: Small raises in Y, T, W and I shapes strengthen the muscles that control the shoulder blade, especially the lower traps that are often weak in rounded posture. Poliquin's structural balance and Cressey's shoulder programmes rely on them.
Cue 1: Chest supported on an incline bench or lying face down
Cue 2: Thumbs up, lift the arms into the shape using the shoulder blades
Cue 3: Pause 1 to 2s at the top, lower slowly
Common faults: Shrugging up to the ears; Using heavy weights and swinging; Arching the low back
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); DB Sumo Squat (G2); KB Sumo Squat (G2)
Progress by: Light DBs, longer pauses
Regress by: Bodyweight, smaller range
Same level swaps: Plate Front Raise; TRX Y Raise; TRX T Raise
Joint notes: Shoulder rehab friendly. Use 1 to 3kg or bodyweight.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 8 to 12 per shape, pause at the top

Why: Holding the TRX lets people counterbalance, so they can sit deeper and more upright than they could alone. It is the go to G1 squat for beginners, seniors, heavy members and anyone with knee or hip pain, and it builds confidence fast.
Variation notes: Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress).
Cue 1: Hold the handles at chest height with arms straight
Cue 2: Sit back and down, letting the straps take a little weight
Cue 3: Use the legs to stand, the arms only steady you
Common faults: Pulling with the arms to stand up; Leaning back so far the feet slide; Squatting deeper than the pain free range
Progress to: Barbell Box Squat (G2); Goblet Squat (KB) (G2); Goblet Squat (DB) (G2)
Progress by: Use the straps less, slower tempo, add a pause, progress to goblet box squat
Regress by: Squat to a high box with the TRX, reduce depth
Same level swaps: TRX Pull Up Assisted Squat; Box Squat; Goblet Box Squat
Joint notes: Very joint friendly. Ideal first squat after injury or replacement surgery (within surgeon's limits).
Default prescription: 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0
Coach sources: Cosgrove (regress to progress), Boyle, Squat University

Why: The landmine's arc lets people lean into the bar and squat with an upright torso and a guided path. It is very back and shoulder friendly and a great bridge between goblet and barbell squatting.
Variation notes: Landmine: the arc path is shoulder and back friendly and very easy to learn.
Cue 1: Hold the end of the bar at the chest, lean slightly into it
Cue 2: Feet slightly in front of the body, sit down and back
Cue 3: Drive up into the bar, finish tall
Common faults: Feet too close to the bar so the knees jam; Rounding the back; Pushing the bar away with the arms
Progress to: Landmine Squat to Press (G3); Zercher Squat (G3); DB Front Squat (G3)
Progress by: Add plates, add a press at the top, pause reps
Regress to: Wall Sit (G1); Box Squat (G1); Frog Squat (G1)
Regress by: Lighter load, reduce depth, goblet box squat
Same level swaps: Landmine Hack Squat
Joint notes: Shoulder friendly (no bar on the back). Hack squat version loads knees more: control depth with knee pain.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Categories: SQUAT PATTERN: BILATERAL; REHAB: LOWER BACK
Why: A simple, joint friendly way to build quad strength and endurance with zero technique demand. Isometrics can reduce knee pain and are ideal for beginners, seniors and anyone who cannot yet squat through full range. The Swiss ball version lets people practise the squat path with support.
Cue 1: Back flat against the wall, feet hip width and slightly in front
Cue 2: Slide down until the knees are at a pain free angle (aim 90 degrees over time)
Cue 3: Weight through the whole foot, breathe slowly, knees in line with toes
Common faults: Hands pushing on the thighs; Knees caving in; Going too deep too soon and aggravating knees
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); DB Sumo Squat (G2); KB Sumo Squat (G2)
Progress by: Lower the position, hold longer, hold a plate, progress to single leg wall sit or tempo goblet squats
Regress by: Higher position, shorter holds, hands on thighs for the first few sessions
Same level swaps: Isometric Wall Sit; Isometric Squat Hold; Swiss Ball Wall Squat
Joint notes: Very knee friendly at higher positions. Adjust depth to stay at or below 3/10 pain. Avoid long holds with breath holding for members with high blood pressure.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 45s holds, rest 60s, about 70% effort
Coach sources: Squat University, Rehab research (isometrics), Ben Patrick

Why: The classic heavy squat. Builds strength, muscle and bone density (LIFTMOR used heavy squats). Pin and Anderson squats start from the bottom, removing the bounce and building strength out of the hole. At Optimal it is a G4 lift for members with good mobility and no back or shoulder restriction; the SSB is the default alternative.
Variation notes: Barbell: allows the heaviest loading for maximum strength and bone stimulus; earn it with technique (usually G3 to G4, Teams).
Cue 1: Bar on the upper back, hands tight, elbows under the bar
Cue 2: Big breath and brace, sit between the hips with knees tracking the toes
Cue 3: Drive up keeping the chest and hips rising together
Common faults: Hips shooting up first (good morning squat); Losing the brace and rounding at the bottom; Knees caving under load
Progress by: Add load, pause reps, tempo, 1.25 reps, rep maxes (Teams G4 only)
Regress to: Zercher Squat (G3); DB Front Squat (G3); SSB Squat (G3)
Regress by: SSB squat, box squat, goblet or double KB front squat
Same level swaps: Anderson Squat; Tempo Back Squat; Paused Back Squat
Joint notes: High spinal load. Not for active back pain. Needs shoulder external rotation to hold the bar: use SSB or trap bar squat if shoulders are cranky.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
Group alternative: Teams only (heavy or high skill): in groups use a G3 regression from the Regress to list
Coach sources: DeFranco, Squat University, LIFTMOR research, Poliquin

Muscles: Quads, glutes, adductors, upper back, core
Why: Holding the weight at the chest counterbalances the body, so people naturally squat more upright and deeper with better form. Dan John and Squat University both use it as THE teaching squat, and it is strong enough to stay useful for years. Fits groups perfectly because load scales from a 4kg KB to a 40kg+ DB.
Cue 1: Hold the bell tight to the chest, elbows pointing down
Cue 2: Push the knees out and sit between the hips, chest proud
Cue 3: Drive up through the whole foot, squeeze the glutes at the top
Common faults: Rounding the upper back and letting the weight pull you forward; Heels lifting; Knees caving inward on the way up
Progress to: Paused Goblet Squat (G3); 1.5 Rep Goblet Squat (G3)
Progress by: Add load, tempo (4-1-1-0), pause at the bottom, 1.5 reps, move to double KB front squat or SSB squat
Regress to: Goblet Box Squat (G1); Box Squat (G1); TRX Assisted Squat (G1)
Regress by: Goblet squat to a box, TRX assisted squat, lighter bell
Same level swaps: Goblet Squat (DB); Tempo Goblet Squat; Cable Goblet Squat
Joint notes: Knee and back friendly. Heels elevated version helps stiff ankles. Use a box for depth control with knee pain. Upper back can fatigue first as loads get heavy.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
Coach sources: Dan John, Squat University, Cosgrove, Boyle

Why: Front loading keeps the torso upright, puts more work on the quads and core, and puts less shear on the low back than back squatting. The double KB front squat is a great G3 group squat; the barbell front squat is a G4 strength lift for those with the wrist and thoracic mobility.
Variation notes: Barbell: allows the heaviest loading for maximum strength and bone stimulus; earn it with technique (usually G3 to G4, Teams).
Cue 1: Bells or bar in a tight rack, elbows high and forward
Cue 2: Brace, sit straight down between the hips
Cue 3: Keep the elbows up as you drive up
Common faults: Elbows dropping and the chest falling forward; Wrists bent back painfully (barbell); Losing tension at the bottom
Progress by: Add load, pause at the bottom, tempo, progress DB → double KB → barbell front squat
Regress to: Zercher Squat (G3); DB Front Squat (G3)
Regress by: Goblet squat, box to control depth, lighter load
Same level swaps: Paused Front Squat; Double KB Front Rack Squat
Joint notes: Low back friendlier than back squats. Barbell front rack needs wrist, lat and T spine mobility. Zercher loads the elbows: use padding.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
Group alternative: Teams only (heavy or high skill): in groups use a G3 regression from the Regress to list

Cue 1: Brace, shoulder blade pulls first, then the elbow
Cue 2: Row towards the hip (lats) or lower ribs (upper back)
Cue 3: Pause, lower slowly to a full stretch

Why: A simple, joint friendly way to build quad strength and endurance with zero technique demand. Isometrics can reduce knee pain and are ideal for beginners, seniors and anyone who cannot yet squat through full range. The Swiss ball version lets people practise the squat path with support.

Cue 1: Back flat against the wall, feet hip width and slightly in front
Cue 2: Slide down until the knees are at a pain free angle (aim 90 degrees over time)

Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Coach sources: DeFranco, Squat University, LIFTMOR research, Poliquin

Cue 3: Sit back down slowly with control, don't flop
Common faults: Using the hands to push off; Feet too far forward; Collapsing back down onto the seat
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); DB Sumo Squat (G2); KB Sumo Squat (G2)

Regress by: Raise the seat, use hands on thighs or a TRX for help, reduce reps
Same level swaps: Sit to Stand (Chair); Fast Sit to Stand (Power)
Joint notes: Suitable for almost everyone. Raise the seat height for painful knees or hips. Single leg version needs good knee control.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps (or max reps in 30s for testing), stand up fast, lower slowly
Coach sources: Seniors research (functional testing), Gambetta (fundamental movement), Attia (centenarian decathlon)

Cue 2: Slowly lower the other heel towards the floor by bending the working knee forward over the toes

Cue 1: Hike the bell back high between the thighs
Cue 2: Snap the hips forward, squeeze the glutes, let the bell float to chest height

Why: Stepping back and across challenges the hips in a different plane, hitting the side glutes and inner thighs. Good variety and good for hip stability and golf.

Exercise: Shoulder Elevated Single Leg Bridge March
Why: Bridges and hip thrusts train the glutes at their strongest point (full hip extension) with almost no spinal load. They are essential for back pain, knee pain, posture, sprinting and golf power, and are safe for nearly everyone. Single leg versions fix imbalances.
Cue 1: Feet flat, shins vertical at the top
Cue 2: Tuck the ribs down, drive through the heels and squeeze the glutes to lift
Cue 3: Pause at the top without arching the low back, lower slowly

Why: Hamstrings both extend the hip and bend the knee; curls train the knee bending role that RDLs miss. Strong hamstrings protect knees and reduce hamstring strain risk. Nordic curls are among the best researched injury prevention exercises.

Why: Strengthens the back extensors and glutes, improving posture and back resilience. Reverse hypers decompress the spine as they train. Extend to neutral only: the goal is a strong, straight spine, not arching.
Cue 1: Hinge at the hips, keep the spine long
Cue 2: Lift to a straight line from head to heels using the glutes
Cue 3: Lower with control
Common faults: Hyperextending at the top; Swinging/using momentum; Rounding heavily at the bottom under load

Regress to: Prone Cobra (Chek) (G2); Reverse Hyper (Bench) (G2); Superman (Alternating) (G2)

Muscles: Glutes, hamstrings, core, grip, cardiovascular system
Why: The king of hinge conditioning (Dan John, Pavel). Trains explosive hip extension (power) and heart rate at the same time with no impact on the knees. Excellent for fat loss, posture and glute strength. Dead stop versions teach control; single arm versions add anti rotation.
Variation notes: One sided loading adds an anti rotation / anti lateral flexion core challenge and exposes left/right differences.
Cue 1: Hike the bell back high between the thighs
Cue 2: Snap the hips forward, squeeze the glutes, let the bell float to chest height
Cue 3: Let it fall, hinge late, keep the spine neutral
Common faults: Squatting the swing instead of hinging; Lifting with the arms; Leaning back at the top
Progress to: Double KB Clean (G4); KB High Pull (Single Arm) (G4); Barbell Push Jerk (G4)
Progress by: Heavier bell, single arm, alternating, swings EMOM, heavier with fewer reps for power
Regress to: KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2); American KB Swing (G2)

Same level swaps: Double KB Swing; Single Arm KB Swing to Catch; Single Arm KB Swing (Anti Rotation)
Joint notes: Back friendly when the hinge is good. Teach the KB deadlift first. Not for acute low back pain. American (overhead) swings stress shoulders and low back: use hip height swings instead.
Default prescription: 4 to 10 sets x 10 to 20 reps, or EMOM; 'hike, snap, float'

Why: Cable/band pull throughs teach the hip hinge with the load pulling from behind, so people naturally sit the hips back and finish with the glutes. Kickbacks and quadruped hip extensions isolate the glutes for activation and rehab.
Variation notes: Cable: constant tension through the whole range with smooth, joint friendly resistance.
Cue 1: Face away from the cable, rope between the legs
Cue 2: Hinge back letting the rope pull the hips back
Cue 3: Drive the hips through and squeeze the glutes, stand tall
Common faults: Pulling with the arms; Squatting instead of hinging; Leaning back at the top
Progress to: Single Arm Cable Pull Through (G2); KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2)
Progress by: Heavier, pause at the top, progress to KB swing
Regress by: Band version, shorter range
Same level swaps: Cable Kickback; Band Pull Through; Cable Pull Through
Joint notes: Very back friendly. A great swing and deadlift regression.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8

Muscles: Chest, shoulders, triceps, serratus, core (anti extension)
Why: A moving plank: chest and arm strength plus core control. The shoulder blades move freely, which is healthier for shoulders than bench pressing. Easy to scale by hand height so every level in a group can do the same exercise. Push up plus adds serratus work for shoulder health.
Cue 1: Hands just outside shoulders, body in a straight line, glutes and abs tight
Cue 2: Lower the chest between the hands, elbows about 45 degrees from the body
Cue 3: Push the floor away until arms are straight and the upper back is spread
Common faults: Hips sagging; Elbows flaring to 90 degrees; Head poking forward / half reps
Progress to: Press Up (G2); TRX Press Up (G2); Wide Press Up (G2)
Progress by: Lower the hand height (wall → bench → box → floor), tempo, pause, feet elevated, add a weighted vest/plate
Regress by: Higher incline (bench or wall), knee push up, shorter range
Same level swaps: Box Press Up; Knee Press Up; Incline Press Up (Bench)
Joint notes: Wrist pain: use DB handles or fists. Shoulder pain: elevate the hands and keep elbows tucked.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 6 to 15 reps (or total reps progression)

Why: Dumbbells let each arm move freely and the shoulders find their own path, so they are friendlier for 40+ shoulders than a straight bar. Neutral grip (palms facing) is the most shoulder friendly; squeeze presses bias the chest with lighter loads; single arm versions add core.
Cue 1: Shoulder blades back and down
Cue 2: Lower with elbows about 45 degrees, forearms vertical
Cue 3: Press up together without clanking the bells
Common faults: Flaring elbows; Dropping too deep with tight shoulders; Arching the low back off the bench
Progress to: DB Bench Press (G3); DB Floor Press (G3); Alternating DB Bench Press (G3)
Progress by: Heavier, single arm, alternating, tempo, incline angle changes
Regress to: Box Press Up (G1); Wall Press Up (G1); Knee Press Up (G1)
Regress by: Floor press, lighter weight, push up variation
Same level swaps: DB Incline Press; Swiss Ball DB Press; DB Low Incline Press
Joint notes: Neutral grip and floor presses protect shoulders. Single arm versions: brace hard.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Why: The landmine press moves on an arc between a horizontal and vertical press, letting the shoulder blade move freely. It is the most shoulder friendly way to press overhead and the go to for members who can't press straight overhead (Cressey). Half kneeling adds core and hip stability.

Cue 3: Lower with control back to the shoulder

Progress by: Half kneeling → tall kneeling → split stance → standing → push press; add plates
Regress to: Landmine Press (Light) (G1); Seated DB Shoulder Press (G1)
Regress by: Lighter, two hands, half kneeling
Same level swaps: Landmine Press; Landmine Push Press; Landmine Chest Press
Joint notes: Best press for shoulder pain and limited overhead range.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each arm)

Exercise: Half Kneeling Single Arm DB Press
Why: Pressing overhead builds shoulder strength and the ability to put things on high shelves (a real life task). LIFTMOR used overhead presses for spinal bone density. Requires overhead mobility; half kneeling and single arm versions add core demand and are often easier on the low back.
Variation notes: One sided loading adds an anti rotation / anti lateral flexion core challenge and exposes left/right differences. Kneeling position locks the hips so the core has to control the trunk and stops the legs cheating.
Cue 1: Ribs down, glutes tight, wrist stacked over the elbow
Cue 2: Press up and slightly back so the biceps finish by the ears
Cue 3: Lower with control to the shoulder
Common faults: Arching the low back to get the weight up; Pressing forward; Shrugging at the top
Progress to: Barbell Thruster (G4); Z Press (Barbell) (G4)
Progress by: Seated → half kneeling → standing → push press; heavier, single arm, bottoms up
Regress to: Arnold Press (G2); DB Push Press (G2); Split Stance DB Press (G2)
Regress by: Landmine press, high incline DB press, lighter weights
Same level swaps: Z Press (DB); Offset DB Press; Single Arm DB Press (Standing)
Joint notes: Needs pain free overhead range (wall test). Shoulder pain: landmine press. Behind the neck pressing: avoid for 40+.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
Coach sources: Cressey, Poliquin, LIFTMOR research, Dan John

Why: The ultimate upper body bodyweight strength test. Hangs build grip (a strong predictor of longevity) and decompress the spine; negatives and isometrics build strength for the first pull up. LIFTMOR used jumping chin ups with drop landings for bone.
Variation notes: Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
Cue 1: Grip slightly wider than shoulders (chin up: palms facing you)
Cue 2: Pull the shoulder blades down first, then drive the elbows to the ribs
Cue 3: Chin over the bar, lower slowly to straight arms
Common faults: Kipping or swinging; Half reps; Shrugging at the bottom
Progress to: Weighted Pull Up (G4); Weighted Chin Up (G4); Commando Pull Up (G4)
Progress by: Band assisted → negatives → bodyweight → weighted
Regress to: Hanging (Supported) (G2); TRX Assisted Pull Up (G2); Band Assisted Pull Up (G2)
Regress by: Lat pulldown, TRX assisted pull up, scapula pull up, dead hang
Same level swaps: Pull Up; Chin Up; Dead Hang
Joint notes: Shoulder pain: neutral grip, band assistance. Hanging can irritate some shoulders: build up gradually.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 or total reps

Muscles: Upper back, lats, rear shoulders, biceps, grip

Variation notes: Cable: constant tension through the whole range with smooth, joint friendly resistance.
Cue 1: Brace, shoulder blade pulls first, then the elbow
Cue 2: Row towards the hip (lats) or lower ribs (upper back)
Cue 3: Pause, lower slowly to a full stretch

Progress to: Single Arm Cable Row (G3); Split Stance Single Arm Cable Row (G3); Single Arm Cable Row with Rotation (G3)

Regress by: Chest supported row, cable row, TRX row
Same level swaps: Cable High Row; Seated Cable Row; Cable Squat to Row
Joint notes: Chest supported and cable versions are the most back friendly. Bent over versions load the low back: avoid pairing with RDLs for 40+.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Regress by: Smaller range
Same level swaps: Shrug to Retraction; Scapula Retraction (TRX)

Why: Holding the TRX lets people counterbalance, so they can sit deeper and more upright than they could alone. It is the go to G1 squat for beginners, seniors, heavy members and anyone with knee or hip pain, and it builds confidence fast.

Pattern: Carry / gait: sled push, pull and drag
Muscles: Quads, glutes, calves, whole body conditioning
Why: The sled is the most joint friendly strength and conditioning tool in the gym: concentric only, so almost no soreness, no impact and no technique to fail. Ben Patrick uses backward drags for knee health; DeFranco uses pushes for conditioning. Every member at every level can use it.
Cue 1: Push: arms extended or bent, body at 45 degrees, drive through the balls of the feet
Cue 2: Drag backward: lean back, small steps, push through the front of the foot (knees over toes)
Cue 3: Keep steady steps and a neutral spine
Common faults: Hips too high or too low; Rounding the back; Taking huge steps that slow the sled
Progress to: Prowler Push (G3); Sled Sprint (Push) (G3); Sled Sprint (Pull) (G3)
Progress by: More weight, faster (sprints), longer distance, less rest
Regress by: Lighter, slower, shorter distance
Same level swaps: Sled Push; Sled Pull; Sled Row (Rope)
Joint notes: Almost universally safe. Backward drag is a knee pain staple. Heavy pushes raise blood pressure: keep breathing.
Default prescription: 6 to 10 x 15 to 25m, walk back recovery; or 3 to 5 min backward drag in warm up

Cue 1: Elbows under shoulders, straight line head to heels
Cue 2: Squeeze glutes, pull the ribs down, push the floor away
Cue 3: Breathe, hold with full tension
Common faults: Sagging hips; Bum in the air; Holding for minutes with poor form
Progress to: Single Arm Plank (G3); Long Lever Plank (G3)
Progress by: Long lever, RKC plank, leg lift, body saw
Regress to: Dead Bug (G1); Plank on Knees (G1); Dead Bug Heel Taps (G1)
Regress by: Plank on knees, incline plank on a bench
Same level swaps: Plank Saw; RKC Plank; Front Plank
Joint notes: Shoulder or wrist pain: dead bug or Pallof press instead. Prefer 20 to 30s high tension holds over long sloppy ones.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 20 to 40s (high tension)

Why: A real life movement (stairs, kerbs, climbing). Very back friendly, easy to scale by box height, and the concentric emphasis means little soreness. Knee drive and crossover versions add balance and hip work.

Cue 2: Lean forward slightly and drive through the box leg to stand tall
Cue 3: Step down with control, don't push off the bottom leg
Common faults: Pushing off the floor leg; Knee caving as you stand; Box too high so the hip hikes
Progress to: Barbell Step Up (G3); Step Up to Single Leg RDL (G3)
Progress by: Higher box, add DBs/goblet/barbell, add a knee drive, slower lowering
Regress to: Patrick Step (G1); Poliquin Step Up (G1); Petersen Step Up (G1)
Regress by: Lower box, hand support, bodyweight
Same level swaps: DB Step Up; Goblet Step Up; Lateral Step Up
Joint notes: Knee friendly at lower heights. Use a low box and hand support for seniors and knee pain. Faster 'step ups' in BURN keep impact low.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)

Cue 2: Back flat, move opposite hand and foot together
Cue 3: Small steps, keep the hips still
Common faults: Hips high; Back rounding; Moving too fast

Regress to: Monster Walk (G1); Sled Lateral Drag (G1); Lateral Sled Push (G1)
Regress by: Static bear hold, knees down
Same level swaps: Crab Walk; Bear Crawl; KB Bear Crawl Drag
Joint notes: Wrist pain: use fists or DB handles.
Default prescription: 3 x 20 to 40s or 10 to 20m

Pattern: Power: medicine ball throws and slams
Muscles: Whole body power, rotational core (rotational throws), shoulders
Why: Med ball throws are the safest way to train power for 40+ members: no catching heavy loads, no landing impact, and you can throw as hard as possible. Rotational throws (scoop toss, shot put) are THE golf power exercise (Gambetta, Chek). Wall balls combine a squat with a throw for conditioning.
Cue 1: Load the hips (or rotate back through the hips for rotational throws)
Cue 2: Explode from the ground up: legs, hips, then arms
Cue 3: Throw with intent every rep, reset between reps
Common faults: Throwing with arms only; Rounding the back on slams; Doing so many reps that it becomes slow cardio
Progress to: DB Clean (G3); KB Clean (G3); DB Snatch (G3)
Progress by: Heavier ball, more distance/speed, step into the throw, single leg stance
Regress to: Monster Walk (G1); Sled Lateral Drag (G1); Lateral Sled Push (G1)
Regress by: Lighter ball, half kneeling throw, slower controlled chops
Same level swaps: Wall Balls; Med Ball Slam; Med Ball Side Slam
Joint notes: Low impact and joint friendly. Use a soft ball for slams. Rotational throws: avoid with acute back pain. Wall balls need shoulder overhead range.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 sets x 3 to 6 reps, full recovery (60 to 120s), stop when speed drops (each side for rotational)

Muscles: Glute medius and minimus, hip stabilisers

Cue 1: Athletic stance, band around the knees or ankles
Cue 2: Push the knees out, step sideways (or lift the leg) leading with the heel
Cue 3: Stay low and keep the pelvis level
Common faults: Rocking the torso side to side; Feet turning out; Letting the band pull the knees in
Progress to: Single Leg Glute Bridge (Mini Band) (G2); Cossack Squat (G2); Paused Hip Thrust (G2)
Progress by: Heavier band, band lower on the leg, side plank abduction
Regress by: Side lying with no band, smaller range
Same level swaps: Monster Walk; Crab Walk (Mini Band); Clam Shell (Mini Band)
Joint notes: Very joint friendly, ideal for hip and knee rehab.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 20 each side

Cue 1: Hike the bell back high between the thighs
Cue 2: Snap the hips forward, squeeze the glutes, let the bell float to chest height
Cue 3: Let it fall, hinge late, keep the spine neutral
Common faults: Squatting the swing instead of hinging; Lifting with the arms; Leaning back at the top
Progress to: Double KB Clean (G4); KB High Pull (Single Arm) (G4); Barbell Push Jerk (G4)
Progress by: Heavier bell, single arm, alternating, swings EMOM, heavier with fewer reps for power
Regress to: KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2); American KB Swing (G2)
Regress by: KB deadlift, dead stop swing, lighter bell, cable pull through
Same level swaps: Double KB Swing; Single Arm KB Swing; Single Arm KB Swing to Catch
Joint notes: Back friendly when the hinge is good. Teach the KB deadlift first. Not for acute low back pain. American (overhead) swings stress shoulders and low back: use hip height swings instead.
Default prescription: 4 to 10 sets x 10 to 20 reps, or EMOM; 'hike, snap, float'

Why: Diagonal patterns that link the hips and shoulders through the core (Paul Chek's twist pattern, Gray Cook's chops and lifts). Train controlled rotation and are a staple of golf programmes.
Variation notes: Cable: constant tension through the whole range with smooth, joint friendly resistance. Kneeling position locks the hips so the core has to control the trunk and stops the legs cheating.
Cue 1: Feet stable, brace
Cue 2: Pull the cable diagonally across the body, letting the hips and upper back turn together
Cue 3: Control the return
Common faults: All arms; Twisting only at the low back; Too heavy and jerky
Progress to: Single Arm Cable Row with Rotation (G3); Bird Dog Row (G3); Single Arm Plank (G3)
Progress by: Standing, heavier, with a step, faster (power)
Regress to: Pallof Press (Cable) (G1); Pallof Press (G1); Pallof Walkout (G1)
Regress by: Half/tall kneeling, lighter, smaller range
Same level swaps: Band Woodchop; Cable Lift with Step; Half Kneeling Cable Chop
Joint notes: Keep rotation through the hips and upper back, not the lumbar spine. Half kneeling is most back friendly.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 6 to 10 reps each side (or 20 to 40s), slow and controlled

Exercise: Single Arm Cable Row with Rotation
Muscles: Upper back, lats, rear shoulders, biceps, grip
Why: Rows build the upper back that holds posture upright and balances pressing. Chest supported rows remove the low back from the equation; single arm rows allow heavier loading and fix imbalances; bent over rows add hinge endurance. Aim for about 2 pulls for every push in desk based members.
Variation notes: One sided loading adds an anti rotation / anti lateral flexion core challenge and exposes left/right differences. Cable: constant tension through the whole range with smooth, joint friendly resistance. Combination move: trains two qualities at once, efficient for HYBRID and BURN; keep technique of both parts clean before speeding up.
Cue 1: Brace, shoulder blade pulls first, then the elbow
Cue 2: Row towards the hip (lats) or lower ribs (upper back)
Cue 3: Pause, lower slowly to a full stretch
Common faults: Jerking and twisting the torso; Shrugging; Shortening the range
Progress by: Heavier, pause at the top, tempo, single arm, 1.5 reps
Regress to: Cable High Row (G2); Seated Cable Row (G2); Cable Squat to Row (G2)
Regress by: Chest supported row, cable row, TRX row
Same level swaps: Single Arm Cable Row; Split Stance Single Arm Cable Row; Single Arm DB Row
Joint notes: Chest supported and cable versions are the most back friendly. Bent over versions load the low back: avoid pairing with RDLs for 40+.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Joint notes: Wrist pain: use DB handles or fists. Shoulder pain: elevate the hands and keep elbows tucked.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 6 to 15 reps (or total reps progression)

Muscles: Thoracic spine rotation and extension, lats, pecs
Why: The upper back should move; the low back should be stable (joint by joint). Stiff upper backs cause rounded posture, shoulder pain and low back pain, and limit the golf swing. Daily T spine drills fix it.
Cue 1: Keep the hips still (knee pinned or in quadruped)
Cue 2: Rotate/extend through the upper back, follow the hand with the eyes
Cue 3: Breathe out into the end range
Common faults: Rotating from the low back; Rushing; Forcing range

Default prescription: 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down

Pattern: Power: medicine ball throws and slams
Muscles: Whole body power, rotational core (rotational throws), shoulders
Why: Med ball throws are the safest way to train power for 40+ members: no catching heavy loads, no landing impact, and you can throw as hard as possible. Rotational throws (scoop toss, shot put) are THE golf power exercise (Gambetta, Chek). Wall balls combine a squat with a throw for conditioning.
Cue 1: Load the hips (or rotate back through the hips for rotational throws)
Cue 2: Explode from the ground up: legs, hips, then arms
Cue 3: Throw with intent every rep, reset between reps
Common faults: Throwing with arms only; Rounding the back on slams; Doing so many reps that it becomes slow cardio
Progress to: DB Clean (G3); KB Clean (G3); DB Snatch (G3)
Progress by: Heavier ball, more distance/speed, step into the throw, single leg stance
Regress to: KB Halo (G1); Bird Dog (G1); Plate Halo (G1)
Regress by: Lighter ball, half kneeling throw, slower controlled chops
Same level swaps: Wall Balls; Med Ball Slam; Med Ball Side Slam
Joint notes: Low impact and joint friendly. Use a soft ball for slams. Rotational throws: avoid with acute back pain. Wall balls need shoulder overhead range.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 sets x 3 to 6 reps, full recovery (60 to 120s), stop when speed drops (each side for rotational)

Why: The safest way to teach lifting from the floor. Picking things up is a life skill (Primal Pattern 'bend'). Raising the bell on blocks reduces range for beginners and back pain; suitcase versions add anti lateral flexion.

Cue 3: Push the floor away and stand tall, squeeze the glutes

Regress by: Bell on a block/step, hinge drill
Same level swaps: KB Deadlift; DB Deadlift; Sumo KB Deadlift

Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Pattern: Power: medicine ball throws and slams

Cue 1: Load the hips (or rotate back through the hips for rotational throws)
Cue 2: Explode from the ground up: legs, hips, then arms
Cue 3: Throw with intent every rep, reset between reps

Why: Holding the weight in front forces the core to resist being pulled forward and the upper back to stay upright. Great posture and core work.

Cue 1: Weight tight to the chest
Cue 2: Stand tall, ribs down, walk slowly
Cue 3: Breathe behind the brace
Common faults: Leaning back to counterbalance; Holding the breath; Elbows drifting
Progress by: Heavier, double KB, uneven
Regress to: Goblet Carry (G2); Duck Walk (KB Goblet) (G2); Front Rack Carry (Single KB) (G2)
Regress by: Lighter, goblet
Same level swaps: Front Rack Hold (Double KB); Front Rack Carry (Double KB); Zercher Carry (Barbell)
Joint notes: Generally safe. Duck walks are deep knee bending: knee pain caution.

Exercise: Battle Rope Side to Side Waves
Why: Upper body conditioning with no impact. Great in BURN circuits and for members who can't run or jump.
Cue 1: Athletic stance, brace
Cue 2: Drive the waves from the shoulders and hips
Cue 3: Keep a steady rhythm
Common faults: Standing upright and stiff; Shrugging; Waves dying out
Progress to: Bird Dog Row (G3); Single Arm Plank (G3); Offset Front Rack Carry (G3)
Progress by: Longer, faster, heavier rope
Regress to: KB Halo (G1); Bird Dog (G1); Plate Halo (G1)
Regress by: Shorter intervals, kneeling
Same level swaps: Battle Rope Slams; Battle Rope Rainbows; Battle Rope Double Waves

Muscles: Quads, glutes, hamstrings, balance, grip when loaded

Cue 2: Drop the back knee down, front knee over the middle of the foot
Cue 3: Push through the front foot and step through to the next rep

Progress to: Barbell Walking Lunge (G3); Overhead Walking Lunge (KB) (G3); Overhead Walking Lunge (Plate) (G3)
Progress by: Add load (DB, KB rack, overhead), pulses, longer distance
Regress to: Split Squat (Supported) (G1); Split Squat (Bodyweight) (G1); TRX Assisted Split Squat (G1)
Regress by: Reverse lunge, split squat, hand support
Same level swaps: TRX Lunge; Lunge Pulses; Forward Lunge (DB)

Coach sources: Gambetta (lunge matrix), Cosgrove, Paul Chek (lunge pattern)

Why: Diagonal patterns that link the hips and shoulders through the core (Paul Chek's twist pattern, Gray Cook's chops and lifts). Train controlled rotation and are a staple of golf programmes.

Why: Lowering and raising the legs while keeping the low back down trains lower abdominal control. Hanging versions add grip and are advanced.

Why: Dynamic core exercises that pull the knees or hips up from a plank or lying position. Good for conditioning and variety at higher levels.

Cue 2: Pull the knees or hips up with the abs
Cue 3: Return with control

Why: Classic ab exercises. They work the abs but repeated loaded spinal flexion is not ideal for discs, so they are low priority at Optimal compared with anti movement work.

Cue 2: Exhale as you curl
Cue 3: Control the lowering
Common faults: Pulling on the neck; Using momentum; High reps fast
Progress to: Swiss Ball Stir the Pot (G3); V Up (G3); Tuck Up (G3)
Progress by: Weighted, cable
Regress to: Dead Bug (G1); Pelvic Tilt (G1); Bird Dog Hold (G1)

Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8

Why: Dan John says loaded carries change lives. Picking up heavy things and walking trains grip (a strong longevity predictor), posture, core and conditioning all at once, with low technical demand and low injury risk. Every member, every week.

Pattern: Carry / gait: sled push, pull and drag
Muscles: Quads, glutes, calves, whole body conditioning

Cue 1: Push: arms extended or bent, body at 45 degrees, drive through the balls of the feet
Cue 2: Drag backward: lean back, small steps, push through the front of the foot (knees over toes)

Common faults: Hips too high or too low; Rounding the back; Taking huge steps that slow the sled
Progress to: Prowler Push (G3); Sled Sprint (Push) (G3); Sled Sprint (Pull) (G3)
Progress by: More weight, faster (sprints), longer distance, less rest
Regress by: Lighter, slower, shorter distance
Same level swaps: Sled Pull; Sled Row (Rope); Sled Pull (Rope)
Joint notes: Almost universally safe. Backward drag is a knee pain staple. Heavy pushes raise blood pressure: keep breathing.
Default prescription: 6 to 10 x 15 to 25m, walk back recovery; or 3 to 5 min backward drag in warm up

Cue 1: Deadlift the weights up properly
Cue 2: Stand tall, shoulders down, walk with short controlled steps
Cue 3: Breathe and keep the ribs down
Common faults: Shrugging; Leaning forward or side to side; Fast sloppy steps
Progress to: Suitcase Hold (G2); Suitcase March (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2)
Progress by: Heavier, longer, on the toes, with steps/obstacles; Dan John standard: bodyweight total for men
Regress by: Lighter, shorter, static hold
Same level swaps: Farmer's Carry; Farmer's Carry March; Farmer's Hold (Static)
Joint notes: Very safe. Pick up and put down with a good hinge. Grip limited members: straps are fine to train the rest.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 40m (or 30 to 45s), rest 60 to 90s

Why: One side loading turns a carry into an anti lateral flexion core exercise: you must stop the body leaning. McGill calls the suitcase carry one of the best core exercises.
Variation notes: One sided loading adds an anti rotation / anti lateral flexion core challenge and exposes left/right differences.
Cue 1: Weight in one hand, stand tall, shoulders level
Cue 2: Walk slowly without leaning towards or away from the weight
Cue 3: Swap hands
Common faults: Leaning; Shrugging the loaded side; Rushing
Progress to: Single Arm Overhead Carry (DB) (G4)
Progress by: Heavier, march with high knees, longer
Regress to: Suitcase Hold (G2); Suitcase March (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2)
Regress by: Lighter, static hold
Joint notes: Back pain friendly.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 40m (or 30 to 45s), rest 60 to 90s each side

Why: Combining positions, directions and obstacles adds variety and real world challenge.
Cue 1: Change positions with control
Cue 2: Stand tall through every position
Cue 3: Short controlled steps
Common faults: Rushing transitions; Losing posture; Too heavy
Progress to: Uneven Front Rack Carry (G3); Single Arm Farmer's Carry Turn (G3); Bottoms Up KB Carry (G3)
Progress by: Heavier, longer
Regress to: Farmer's Carry March (G1); Farmer's Hold (Static) (G1); Farmer's Carry on Toes (G1)
Regress by: Lighter, single position
Same level swaps: Farmer's Carry Up and Down Step; Mixed Carry (Rack and Suitcase); Mixed Carry (Overhead and Suitcase)
Joint notes: Generally safe.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 40m (or 30 to 45s), rest 60 to 90s

Why: Holding weight overhead while walking trains shoulder stability and core in one. Bottoms up holds make the rotator cuff work hard with light weight: brilliant for shoulder rehab.
Variation notes: One sided loading adds an anti rotation / anti lateral flexion core challenge and exposes left/right differences.
Cue 1: Arm locked, biceps by the ear, shoulder packed
Cue 2: Ribs down, walk slowly
Cue 3: Keep the weight stacked over the shoulder
Common faults: Arching the back; Arm drifting forward; Going too heavy
Progress by: Heavier, double, bottoms up
Regress to: Bottoms Up KB Carry (G3); Overhead Carry (Plate) (G3); Barbell Overhead Carry (G3)
Regress by: Waiter's carry, lighter, static hold
Joint notes: Needs pain free overhead range. Waiter's carry (arm at 90 degrees) is an easier option.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 40m (or 30 to 45s), rest 60 to 90s

Muscles: Whole lower body, tendons, nervous system
Why: Jumps and hops train power, tendon stiffness and bone (impact is a key bone stimulus in LIFTMOR). Progress carefully: landing before jumping, low before high, two legs before one.

Common faults: Landing stiff legged or with knees caving; Too many reps (plyos are not cardio); Progressing too fast
Progress to: Single Leg Box Jump (G4); Alternating Lunge Jump (G4)
Progress by: Landings → small jumps → box jumps → broad jumps → single leg hops → depth jumps
Regress to: Snap Downs (G2); Drop Squat (G2); Pogo Hops (Low) (G2)

Cautions: Knee, Low back, Osteoporosis/osteopenia, Pelvic floor

Group alternative: Group swap (no jumping): sled push, fast step ups, med ball chest pass or slam, KB swing, fast sit to stand

Cue 2: Explode up through the legs and hips, shrug and pull the elbows high
Cue 3: Catch softly in a strong rack position (or overhead), stand tall

Regress to: Med Ball Slam (G2); Slam Ball Slam (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2)
Regress by: Pull only (no catch), KB swing, med ball scoop toss, landmine clean
Same level swaps: DB Clean; KB Clean; DB Snatch
Joint notes: Wrists, shoulders and low back need to be healthy. Barbell versions: Teams G4 only. Not for osteoporosis without careful progression.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 sets x 3 to 6 reps, full recovery (60 to 120s), stop when speed drops

Why: Links a squat and an overhead press into one total body movement. Very metabolic, great for BURN and HYBRID sessions, and the legs help drive the weight overhead so people can press more.

Cue 1: Squat with the weight in the rack
Cue 2: Drive up hard and use that momentum to press overhead
Cue 3: Lock out with biceps by the ears, ribs down, then lower back to the rack

Progress to: Barbell Thruster (G4); Double KB Front Squat to Press (G4); Barbell Front Rack Squat to Press (G4)
Progress by: Add load, double KBs, barbell, more rounds or density
Regress to: Med Ball Slam (G2); Slam Ball Slam (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2)
Regress by: Goblet squat to press, landmine squat to press, split into separate squat and press
Same level swaps: Landmine Squat to Press; DB Thruster; KB Thruster
Joint notes: Needs pain free overhead range. With shoulder pain swap to squat to landmine press. Watch technique as fatigue builds in circuits.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 8 to 12 reps, or 30 to 40s in circuits

Muscles: Upper back, lats, rear shoulders, biceps, grip
Why: Rows build the upper back that holds posture upright and balances pressing. Chest supported rows remove the low back from the equation; single arm rows allow heavier loading and fix imbalances; bent over rows add hinge endurance. Aim for about 2 pulls for every push in desk based members.
Cue 1: Brace, shoulder blade pulls first, then the elbow
Cue 2: Row towards the hip (lats) or lower ribs (upper back)
Cue 3: Pause, lower slowly to a full stretch
Common faults: Jerking and twisting the torso; Shrugging; Shortening the range

Muscles: Glutes, hamstrings, core, grip, cardiovascular system

Pattern: Carry / gait: sled push, pull and drag
Muscles: Quads, glutes, calves, whole body conditioning
Why: The sled is the most joint friendly strength and conditioning tool in the gym: concentric only, so almost no soreness, no impact and no technique to fail. Ben Patrick uses backward drags for knee health; DeFranco uses pushes for conditioning. Every member at every level can use it.
Cue 1: Push: arms extended or bent, body at 45 degrees, drive through the balls of the feet
Cue 2: Drag backward: lean back, small steps, push through the front of the foot (knees over toes)
Cue 3: Keep steady steps and a neutral spine
Common faults: Hips too high or too low; Rounding the back; Taking huge steps that slow the sled
Progress to: Prowler Push (G3); Sled Sprint (Push) (G3); Sled Sprint (Pull) (G3)
Progress by: More weight, faster (sprints), longer distance, less rest
Regress by: Lighter, slower, shorter distance
Same level swaps: Sled Push; Sled Row (Rope); Sled Pull (Rope)
Joint notes: Almost universally safe. Backward drag is a knee pain staple. Heavy pushes raise blood pressure: keep breathing.
Default prescription: 6 to 10 x 15 to 25m, walk back recovery; or 3 to 5 min backward drag in warm up

Why: Ben Patrick's number one knee tool: walking backwards loads the quads with the knee travelling over the toes, floods the knee with blood and is nearly impossible to overdo.
Cue 1: Lean back slightly against the sled (or hold the treadmill rails)
Cue 2: Small steps, push through the front of the foot
Cue 3: Knees travel over the toes
Common faults: Big steps; Standing tall; Too heavy
Progress to: Crab Walk (G2); KB Swings (G2); Bear Crawl (G2)
Progress by: Heavier, longer
Regress by: Lighter, treadmill flat
Same level swaps: Reverse Sled Drag; Sled Drag (Backwards); Backwards Walking (Treadmill Incline)
Joint notes: Knee pain staple. Very safe.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 min warm up, or 4 to 6 x 20m

Why: A real life movement (stairs, kerbs, climbing). Very back friendly, easy to scale by box height, and the concentric emphasis means little soreness. Knee drive and crossover versions add balance and hip work.
Variation notes: Fast/power version: move with intent, stop when speed drops.
Cue 1: Whole foot on the box, knee over the middle of the foot
Cue 2: Lean forward slightly and drive through the box leg to stand tall
Cue 3: Step down with control, don't push off the bottom leg
Common faults: Pushing off the floor leg; Knee caving as you stand; Box too high so the hip hikes
Progress to: Barbell Step Up (G3); Step Up to Single Leg RDL (G3)
Progress by: Higher box, add DBs/goblet/barbell, add a knee drive, slower lowering
Regress to: Patrick Step (G1); Poliquin Step Up (G1); Petersen Step Up (G1)
Regress by: Lower box, hand support, bodyweight
Same level swaps: DB Step Up; Goblet Step Up; Lateral Step Up
Joint notes: Knee friendly at lower heights. Use a low box and hand support for seniors and knee pain. Faster 'step ups' in BURN keep impact low.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)

Progress by: Longer, faster, heavier rope
Regress to: Sled Push (G1); Sled Pull (G1); Rower 500m (G1)
Regress by: Shorter intervals, kneeling
Same level swaps: Battle Rope Slams; Battle Rope Rainbows; Battle Rope Double Waves
Joint notes: Low impact. Rope jumping jacks involve jumping: swap to step jacks in groups.

Muscles: Whole lower body, tendons, nervous system
Why: Jumps and hops train power, tendon stiffness and bone (impact is a key bone stimulus in LIFTMOR). Landings (snap downs, drop squats, jump and stick) teach the body to absorb force, the foundation of injury prevention. Progress carefully: landing before jumping, low before high, two legs before one.
Cue 1: Land softly and quietly, hips back, knees over toes
Cue 2: Stick the landing for a second before the next rep
Cue 3: Quality over quantity: stop when height or control drops
Common faults: Landing stiff legged or with knees caving; Too many reps (plyos are not cardio); Progressing too fast
Progress to: Single Leg Box Jump (G4); Alternating Lunge Jump (G4)
Progress by: Landings → small jumps → box jumps → broad jumps → single leg hops → depth jumps
Regress to: Snap Downs (G2); Drop Squat (G2); Pogo Hops (Low) (G2)
Regress by: Snap downs/drop squat and stick, step ups, sled push, med ball throws
Same level swaps: A Skip; Box Jump; Bounding
Cautions: Knee, Low back, Osteoporosis/osteopenia, Pelvic floor
Joint notes: IMPACT: excluded from Optimal GROUP sessions (no jumping rule). Teams only after screening. Avoid with pelvic floor symptoms, osteoporosis with fracture history, joint replacements, acute knee/Achilles pain.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 sets x 3 to 6 reps, full recovery (60 to 120s), stop when speed drops; 2 to 3 sessions/week max, low total contacts (20 to 60)
Group alternative: Group swap (no jumping): sled push, fast step ups, med ball chest pass or slam, KB swing, fast sit to stand
Coach sources: Gambetta, DeFranco (dynamic effort), LIFTMOR research (impact for bone)

Pattern: Power: medicine ball throws and slams
Muscles: Whole body power, rotational core (rotational throws), shoulders
Why: Med ball throws are the safest way to train power for 40+ members: no catching heavy loads, no landing impact, and you can throw as hard as possible. Rotational throws (scoop toss, shot put) are THE golf power exercise (Gambetta, Chek). Wall balls combine a squat with a throw for conditioning.
Cue 1: Load the hips (or rotate back through the hips for rotational throws)
Cue 2: Explode from the ground up: legs, hips, then arms
Cue 3: Throw with intent every rep, reset between reps
Common faults: Throwing with arms only; Rounding the back on slams; Doing so many reps that it becomes slow cardio
Progress to: DB Clean (G3); KB Clean (G3); DB Snatch (G3)
Progress by: Heavier ball, more distance/speed, step into the throw, single leg stance
Regress to: Sled Push (G1); Sled Pull (G1); Rower 500m (G1)
Regress by: Lighter ball, half kneeling throw, slower controlled chops
Same level swaps: Med Ball Slam; Slam Ball Slam; Med Ball Side Slam
Joint notes: Low impact and joint friendly. Use a soft ball for slams. Rotational throws: avoid with acute back pain. Wall balls need shoulder overhead range.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 sets x 3 to 6 reps, full recovery (60 to 120s), stop when speed drops (each side for rotational)

Cue 2: Chest down (if required), back to feet
Cue 3: Stand tall (jump only if allowed)
Common faults: Sagging plank; Crashing to the floor; Sloppy as fatigue builds
Progress by: Add a press, push up or jump
Regress to: Crab Walk (G2); KB Swings (G2); Bear Crawl (G2)
Regress by: Step back burpee, incline burpee onto a bench
Same level swaps: Step Back Burpee (No Jump); Squat Thrust to Bench (No Jump); Sprawls
Joint notes: IMPACT when jumping: group sessions use the no jump version (step back, step in, stand). Devil's press and man makers: DB hinge skill required.
Default prescription: 3 to 6 x 20 to 40s
Group alternative: Group swap: step back burpee (no jump), squat thrust to a bench, wall ball

Muscles: Glutes, hamstrings, core, grip, cardiovascular system
Why: The king of hinge conditioning (Dan John, Pavel). Trains explosive hip extension (power) and heart rate at the same time with no impact on the knees. Excellent for fat loss, posture and glute strength. Dead stop versions teach control; single arm versions add anti rotation.
Cue 1: Hike the bell back high between the thighs
Cue 2: Snap the hips forward, squeeze the glutes, let the bell float to chest height
Cue 3: Let it fall, hinge late, keep the spine neutral
Common faults: Squatting the swing instead of hinging; Lifting with the arms; Leaning back at the top
Progress to: Double KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing to Catch (G3)
Progress by: Heavier bell, single arm, alternating, swings EMOM, heavier with fewer reps for power
Regress to: KB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1); Elevated KB Deadlift (G1)
Regress by: KB deadlift, dead stop swing, lighter bell, cable pull through
Same level swaps: KB Swing (Power); American KB Swing; KB Dead Stop Swing
Joint notes: Back friendly when the hinge is good. Teach the KB deadlift first. Not for acute low back pain. American (overhead) swings stress shoulders and low back: use hip height swings instead.
Default prescription: 4 to 10 sets x 10 to 20 reps, or EMOM; 'hike, snap, float'

Muscles: Whole lower body, tendons, nervous system
Why: Jumps and hops train power, tendon stiffness and bone (impact is a key bone stimulus in LIFTMOR). Landings (snap downs, drop squats, jump and stick) teach the body to absorb force, the foundation of injury prevention. Progress carefully: landing before jumping, low before high, two legs before one.
Cue 1: Land softly and quietly, hips back, knees over toes
Cue 2: Stick the landing for a second before the next rep
Cue 3: Quality over quantity: stop when height or control drops
Common faults: Landing stiff legged or with knees caving; Too many reps (plyos are not cardio); Progressing too fast
Progress to: Single Leg Box Jump (G4); Alternating Lunge Jump (G4)
Progress by: Landings → small jumps → box jumps → broad jumps → single leg hops → depth jumps
Regress to: Snap Downs (G2); Drop Squat (G2); Pogo Hops (Low) (G2)
Regress by: Snap downs/drop squat and stick, step ups, sled push, med ball throws
Same level swaps: A Skip; Box Jump; Bounding
Cautions: Knee, Low back, Osteoporosis/osteopenia, Pelvic floor
Joint notes: IMPACT: excluded from Optimal GROUP sessions (no jumping rule). Teams only after screening. Avoid with pelvic floor symptoms, osteoporosis with fracture history, joint replacements, acute knee/Achilles pain.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 sets x 3 to 6 reps, full recovery (60 to 120s), stop when speed drops; 2 to 3 sessions/week max, low total contacts (20 to 60)
Group alternative: Group swap (no jumping): sled push, fast step ups, med ball chest pass or slam, KB swing, fast sit to stand
Coach sources: Gambetta, DeFranco (dynamic effort), LIFTMOR research (impact for bone)

Muscles: Upper back, lats, rear shoulders, biceps, core
Why: Pulling your own bodyweight in a plank position. The angle sets the difficulty, so it scales from total beginner (standing upright) to advanced (feet elevated) in the same station. A core Optimal group exercise and part of Ed's screening (TRX row at 45 degrees).
Variation notes: Tempo version: a slow 3 to 5 second lowering builds control, tendon strength and muscle at lighter loads (Poliquin), ideal for joint sensitive members. Fast/power version: move with intent, stop when speed drops.
Cue 1: Body in a straight line, heels down
Cue 2: Pull the chest to the handles, shoulder blades back and down
Cue 3: Lower slowly to straight arms
Common faults: Hips sagging; Shrugging or poking the chin forward; Half reps
Progress to: Single Arm TRX Row (G3); TRX Row (Feet Elevated) (G3); Band Resisted Inverted Row (G3)
Progress by: Walk the feet forward (more horizontal), feet elevated, single arm, pause/tempo
Regress to: Chest Supported DB Row (G1); Chest Supported DB Row (Neutral) (G1)
Regress by: Stand more upright, step back, scapular retraction only (G1 of the Optimal screen)
Same level swaps: TRX Row; Isometric Row Hold (TRX); Inverted Row to Pull Up Progression
Joint notes: Shoulder friendly. Neutral grip TRX handles are easiest on elbows.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 8 to 15 reps (or total reps progression), pause at the top

Why: Low impact, fun, rotational conditioning.
Cue 1: Guard up, rotate through the hips
Cue 2: Snap punches out and back
Cue 3: Stay light on the feet
Common faults: Locking elbows; Arms only; Dropping the guard
Progress to: Crab Walk (G2); KB Swings (G2); Bear Crawl (G2)
Progress by: Faster, light DBs (no lockout)
Regress by: Slower
Joint notes: Low impact.
Default prescription: 3 to 6 x 30 to 60s

Why: Links a squat and an overhead press into one total body movement. Very metabolic, great for BURN and HYBRID sessions, and the legs help drive the weight overhead so people can press more.
Cue 1: Squat with the weight in the rack
Cue 2: Drive up hard and use that momentum to press overhead
Cue 3: Lock out with biceps by the ears, ribs down, then lower back to the rack
Common faults: Pressing before the legs finish the drive; Arching the low back at the top; Losing the rack position and squatting with the elbows dropped
Progress to: Barbell Thruster (G4); Double KB Front Squat to Press (G4); Barbell Front Rack Squat to Press (G4)
Progress by: Add load, double KBs, barbell, more rounds or density
Regress to: DB Complex (G2); Crab Walk (G2); KB Swings (G2)

Same level swaps: DB Thruster; DB Squat to Overhead Press; KB Thruster
Joint notes: Needs pain free overhead range. With shoulder pain swap to squat to landmine press. Watch technique as fatigue builds in circuits.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 8 to 12 reps, or 30 to 40s in circuits

Pattern: Carry / gait: sled push, pull and drag
Muscles: Quads, glutes, calves, whole body conditioning
Why: The sled is the most joint friendly strength and conditioning tool in the gym: concentric only, so almost no soreness, no impact and no technique to fail. Ben Patrick uses backward drags for knee health; DeFranco uses pushes for conditioning. Every member at every level can use it.
Cue 1: Push: arms extended or bent, body at 45 degrees, drive through the balls of the feet
Cue 2: Drag backward: lean back, small steps, push through the front of the foot (knees over toes)
Cue 3: Keep steady steps and a neutral spine
Common faults: Hips too high or too low; Rounding the back; Taking huge steps that slow the sled
Progress to: Prowler Push (G3); Sled Sprint (Push) (G3); Sled Sprint (Pull) (G3)
Progress by: More weight, faster (sprints), longer distance, less rest
Regress by: Lighter, slower, shorter distance
Same level swaps: Sled Push; Sled Pull; Sled Row (Rope)
Joint notes: Almost universally safe. Backward drag is a knee pain staple. Heavy pushes raise blood pressure: keep breathing.
Default prescription: 6 to 10 x 15 to 25m, walk back recovery; or 3 to 5 min backward drag in warm up

Why: Gentle shoulder range of motion work. Pendulums and table slides are first stage rehab for stiff or painful shoulders; dowel and band pass throughs maintain overhead and behind body mobility (DeFranco Simple 6).
Cue 1: Relaxed, no forcing
Cue 2: Move slowly through comfortable range
Cue 3: Breathe
Common faults: Forcing painful range; Shrugging; Arching to fake range
Progress to: Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2); Cross Body Stretch (G2)
Progress by: Bigger range, narrower grip on pass throughs
Regress by: Smaller range, table slides
Same level swaps: Table Slides; Band Dislocates; Dowel Pass Through
Joint notes: Use pain free range only. Frozen shoulder: refer and follow the physio.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down

Why: The serratus holds the shoulder blade against the ribcage and rotates it upward for overhead reaching. Weak serratus = winging and shoulder pain.
Cue 1: Arms straight
Cue 2: Push the floor or weight away, spreading the shoulder blades
Cue 3: Return slowly
Common faults: Bending the elbows; Shrugging; Sagging hips (push up plus)
Progress to: Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2)
Progress by: Push up plus, band punch, heavier
Regress by: Wall version
Same level swaps: Press Up Plus; Scapula Push Up; Serratus Punch (Band)
Joint notes: Very shoulder friendly.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8

Muscles: Target muscles and joints vary (named in the exercise)
Why: Static and gentle mobility work restores range lost from sitting and ageing. Best used where a screen shows a restriction (Squat University: screen, correct, retest), and to cool down. Why: One side loading turns a carry into an anti lateral flexion core exercise: you must stop the body leaning. McGill calls the suitcase carry one of the best core exercises.
Cue 1: Weight in one hand, stand tall, shoulders level
Cue 2: Walk slowly without leaning towards or away from the weight
Cue 3: Swap hands
Common faults: Leaning; Shrugging the loaded side; Rushing
Progress to: Uneven Front Rack Carry (G3); Bottoms Up KB Press (G3); Bottoms Up KB Carry (G3)
Progress by: Heavier, march with high knees, longer
Regress to: Farmer's Carry (G1); Farmer's Carry March (G1); Farmer's Hold (Static) (G1)
Regress by: Lighter, static hold
Same level swaps: Suitcase Hold; Suitcase March; Suitcase Carry
Joint notes: Back pain friendly.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 40m (or 30 to 45s), rest 60 to 90s each side

Pattern: Total body: Turkish get up / windmill
Muscles: Shoulder stability, core, hips, whole body
Why: The get up teaches you to get up from the floor while holding a weight overhead: shoulder stability, hip mobility and confidence in one. Getting off the floor is a key longevity skill (Attia, Dan John, Pavel). Windmills and arm bars build shoulder stability and hip hinge mobility.
Variation notes: Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
Cue 1: Eyes on the bell, arm locked
Cue 2: Move through each step slowly: roll to elbow, hand, high bridge, sweep the leg, kneel, stand
Cue 3: Reverse every step with control
Common faults: Rushing; Bent arm; Losing sight of the bell
Progress to: KB Windmill (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Turkish Get Up (G2)
Progress by: Heavier bell, full get up
Regress by: Half get up, shoe on the fist, no weight
Same level swaps: Half Turkish Get Up
Joint notes: Learn with a shoe or no weight first. Shoulder pain: half get up with no load only.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 reps each side, slow
Coach sources: Dan John, Pavel Tsatsouline, Gray Cook

Why: Pushing into a wall or band without moving loads the shoulder tendons with almost no irritation. First line for painful rotator cuffs.

Cue 2: Push into the wall/band gently and build to about 70%
Cue 3: Hold 30 to 45s, breathe
Common faults: Shrugging; Pushing to pain; Holding the breath

Regress by: Lighter push
Same level swaps: Isometric Internal Rotation; Isometric Shoulder Abduction

Why: The landmine press moves on an arc between a horizontal and vertical press, letting the shoulder blade move freely. It is the most shoulder friendly way to press overhead and the go to for members who can't press straight overhead (Cressey). Half kneeling adds core and hip stability.

Cue 2: Press up and forward, letting the shoulder blade reach around
Cue 3: Lower with control back to the shoulder
Common faults: Arching the low back; Shrugging; Twisting the torso to press
Progress to: Landmine Press (G2); Landmine Push Press (G2); Landmine Chest Press (G2)

Same level swaps: Seated DB Shoulder Press

Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each arm)

Progress to: Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2)
Progress by: Longer holds, deeper range, add loaded stretching
Regress by: Smaller range, supported versions
Same level swaps: Frog Stretch; Couch Stretch; Elephant Walk
Joint notes: Gentle and safe. Stop if symptoms travel down the leg. Osteoporosis: avoid loaded flexion stretches.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
Coach sources: Squat University, DeFranco (Limber 11), Ben Patrick (couch stretch), McGill

Muscles: Rear shoulders, rotator cuff (external rotators), mid traps
Why: Face pulls combine a high row with external rotation, strengthening the muscles that keep shoulders healthy and posture upright. Cressey and DeFranco use them in almost every programme to balance all the pressing. Optimal: at least 2x per week for desk workers.
Cue 1: Rope at forehead height, thumbs pointing back
Cue 2: Pull towards the face, elbows high, separate the rope
Cue 3: Finish with the knuckles beside the ears (like a double bicep pose), pause
Common faults: Leaning back and using bodyweight; Elbows dropping; Shrugging
Progress to: Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2)
Progress by: Heavier, slower, add external rotation emphasis
Regress by: Band face pull, lighter
Same level swaps: TRX Face Pull; Band Face Pull; Cable Face Pull
Joint notes: Shoulder friendly and often therapeutic.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 12 to 20 reps, pause 1s

Categories: REHAB: SHOULDER; MOBILITY AND WARM UP
Why: Slow, full range joint circles under tension. Maintains each joint's usable range and gives a daily joint health check.
Cue 1: Brace everything else
Cue 2: Move the joint through its biggest circle slowly
Cue 3: Keep tension the whole way
Common faults: Compensating with other joints; Rushing; Forcing painful range
Progress to: Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2)
Progress by: Bigger circle, more tension
Regress by: Smaller circle
Same level swaps: Hip CARs; Neck CARs; Standing Hip CARs
Joint notes: Universally safe.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 slow reps each direction

Categories: REHAB: SHOULDER; MOBILITY AND WARM UP
Why: The serratus holds the shoulder blade against the ribcage and rotates it upward for overhead reaching. Weak serratus = winging and shoulder pain.
Cue 1: Arms straight
Cue 2: Push the floor or weight away, spreading the shoulder blades
Cue 3: Return slowly
Common faults: Bending the elbows; Shrugging; Sagging hips (push up plus)
Progress to: Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2)
Progress by: Push up plus, band punch, heavier
Regress by: Wall version
Same level swaps: Press Up Plus; Serratus Punch (Band); Bear Plank Protraction
Joint notes: Very shoulder friendly.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8

Pattern: Vertical pull: pull up / chin up / hangs
Muscles: Lats, upper back, biceps, grip, core
Why: The ultimate upper body bodyweight strength test. Hangs build grip (a strong predictor of longevity) and decompress the spine; negatives and isometrics build strength for the first pull up. LIFTMOR used jumping chin ups with drop landings for bone.
Variation notes: Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress).
Cue 1: Grip slightly wider than shoulders (chin up: palms facing you)
Cue 2: Pull the shoulder blades down first, then drive the elbows to the ribs
Cue 3: Chin over the bar, lower slowly to straight arms
Common faults: Kipping or swinging; Half reps; Shrugging at the bottom
Progress to: Pull Up (G3); Chin Up (G3); Dead Hang (G3)
Progress by: Band assisted → negatives → bodyweight → weighted
Regress to: Scapula Pull Up (G1); Shrug to Retraction (G1); Scapula Retraction (TRX) (G1)
Regress by: Lat pulldown, TRX assisted pull up, scapula pull up, dead hang
Same level swaps: TRX Assisted Pull Up; Band Assisted Pull Up
Joint notes: Shoulder pain: neutral grip, band assistance. Hanging can irritate some shoulders: build up gradually.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 or total reps

Why: Pulldowns train the pull up pattern at any load, essential for members who can't yet do pull ups. Straight arm pulldowns and pullovers isolate the lats, which also helps overhead mobility.
Variation notes: Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
Cue 1: Lean back slightly, chest up
Cue 2: Pull the shoulder blades down then the elbows to the ribs
Cue 3: Return slowly to a full stretch
Common faults: Leaning way back and rowing; Pulling behind the neck (shoulder risk); Shortening the range
Progress to: Band Y Pull (G2); Cable Y Pull (G2); Band Pulldown (G2)
Progress by: Heavier, single arm, tempo, progress to band assisted pull ups
Regress by: Lighter, band pulldown, kneeling
Same level swaps: Chest Supported DB Row; Chest Supported DB Row (Neutral)
Joint notes: Shoulder friendly with neutral grip. Behind the neck versions: avoid for 40+.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Muscles: Mid and lower traps, rhomboids, lats
Why: Training the shoulder blade to move (down, back, up) before the arm pulls. Scapula pull ups and retractions are the first step towards rows and pull ups (G1 of the Optimal row screen).
Cue 1: Arms straight
Cue 2: Move only the shoulder blades
Cue 3: Pause and return
Common faults: Bending the elbows; Shrugging; Rushing
Progress to: Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2)
Progress by: Full rows/pull ups
Regress by: Smaller range
Same level swaps: Scapula Pull Up; Shrug to Retraction
Joint notes: Rehab friendly.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8

Why: Holding weight overhead while walking trains shoulder stability and core in one. Bottoms up holds make the rotator cuff work hard with light weight: brilliant for shoulder rehab.
Variation notes: Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
Cue 1: Arm locked, biceps by the ear, shoulder packed
Cue 2: Ribs down, walk slowly
Cue 3: Keep the weight stacked over the shoulder
Common faults: Arching the back; Arm drifting forward; Going too heavy
Progress to: Overhead Hold (DB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2); Overhead Hold (KB) (G2)
Progress by: Heavier, double, bottoms up
Regress by: Waiter's carry, lighter, static hold
Joint notes: Needs pain free overhead range. Waiter's carry (arm at 90 degrees) is an easier option.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 40m (or 30 to 45s), rest 60 to 90s

Muscles: Foot, ankle, hip stabilisers, nervous system
Why: Balance falls away quickly with age and inactivity; falls are a leading cause of injury in older adults. Single leg balance is part of the Optimal screen. Train it every session for 60+ (Gambetta: postural alignment and dynamic balance are the foundation).
Cue 1: Stand tall near a support
Cue 2: Grip the floor with the foot, soft knee
Cue 3: Hold or reach while keeping the hips level
Common faults: Locking the knee; Holding the breath; Doing it far from support
Progress to: Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Eyes closed, cushion, reach, catch a ball
Regress by: Hand on support, tandem stance
Same level swaps: Heel to Toe Walk; Single Leg Balance; Tandem Stance Balance
Joint notes: Always near a rail or rig for seniors.
Default prescription: 3 x 20 to 30s each leg

Muscles: Glute medius and minimus, hip stabilisers
Why: The side glutes stop the knee caving and the pelvis dropping when on one leg. Weak glute meds are linked to knee pain, hip pain and back pain. Simple band work fixes it and works brilliantly as a warm up (Squat University, Boyle).
Cue 1: Athletic stance, band around the knees or ankles
Cue 2: Push the knees out, step sideways (or lift the leg) leading with the heel
Cue 3: Stay low and keep the pelvis level
Common faults: Rocking the torso side to side; Feet turning out; Letting the band pull the knees in
Progress to: Cossack Squat (G2); Paused Hip Thrust (G2); Lateral Lunge (DB) (G2)
Progress by: Heavier band, band lower on the leg, side plank abduction
Regress by: Side lying with no band, smaller range
Same level swaps: Monster Walk; Reverse Clam; Fire Hydrant
Joint notes: Very joint friendly, ideal for hip and knee rehab.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 20 each side

Why: A real life movement (stairs, kerbs, climbing). Very back friendly, easy to scale by box height, and the concentric emphasis means little soreness. Knee drive and crossover versions add balance and hip work.
Cue 1: Whole foot on the box, knee over the middle of the foot
Cue 2: Lean forward slightly and drive through the box leg to stand tall
Cue 3: Step down with control, don't push off the bottom leg
Common faults: Pushing off the floor leg; Knee caving as you stand; Box too high so the hip hikes
Progress to: Barbell Step Up (G3); Step Up to Single Leg RDL (G3)
Progress by: Higher box, add DBs/goblet/barbell, add a knee drive, slower lowering
Regress to: Patrick Step (G1); Poliquin Step Up (G1); Petersen Step Up (G1)
Regress by: Lower box, hand support, bodyweight
Same level swaps: DB Step Up; Goblet Step Up; Lateral Step Up
Joint notes: Knee friendly at lower heights. Use a low box and hand support for seniors and knee pain. Faster 'step ups' in BURN keep impact low.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)

Muscles: Hamstrings, glutes (incl. glute med), foot and ankle stability
Why: Single leg hinges build hamstring and glute strength, balance and hip stability one side at a time, and they spare the spine because loads are lighter. Kickstand and B stance versions give a stepping stone with the back foot for support. Hip airplanes train hip rotation control (great for golf).
Variation notes: Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress).
Cue 1: Stand on one leg with a soft knee, other leg reaching back
Cue 2: Hinge forward as one straight line from head to heel, hips square
Cue 3: Drive the standing heel into the floor and squeeze the glute to stand
Common faults: Hips opening up (rotating) towards the ceiling; Rounding the back to reach the floor; Standing knee locked straight
Progress to: TRX Single Leg RDL (G3); Single Leg RDL (DB) (G3); Single Leg RDL (KB) (G3)
Progress by: Kickstand → full single leg, add load (DB/KB, double KB, landmine), slower tempo, add a row or reach
Regress to: KB Deadlift (G1); DB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1)
Regress by: Supported single leg RDL (hand on rig), kickstand RDL, bodyweight
Same level swaps: Kickstand RDL; Banded Airplane; Kickstand RDL (DB)
Joint notes: Back friendly. Balance limits load: use a support or kickstand first. Excellent for golfers and runners.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (each leg)
