Why: The entry point of the single leg ladder. A static split stance gives a stable base, so people learn to load one leg at a time safely. It builds balance, fixes imbalances and is far easier on the back than heavy bilateral squats. Front foot elevated adds knee travel (ATG style); cable and landmine versions add stability.
Variation notes: Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress).
Cue 1: Long split stance, both feet pointing forward, hip width apart
Cue 2: Lower the back knee straight down towards the floor
Cue 3: Push through the front foot to stand, keep the torso tall
Common faults: Stance too narrow (tightrope), losing balance; Front heel lifting; Lunging forward instead of dropping down
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); Split Squat (DB) (G2)
Progress by: Add load, elevate the front foot (ATG style), then elevate the back foot (RFESS)
Regress by: TRX or rig assisted split squat, shorter range, isometric split squat hold
Same level swaps: Split Squat (Bodyweight); TRX Assisted Split Squat; Split Squat (Short Range)
Joint notes: Knee friendly when depth is controlled. Use a pad under the back knee. Hold a support for balance in seniors.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)
Coach sources: Boyle, Squat University, Ben Patrick (front foot elevated)

Why: Cable/band pull throughs teach the hip hinge with the load pulling from behind, so people naturally sit the hips back and finish with the glutes. Kickbacks and quadruped hip extensions isolate the glutes for activation and rehab.
Cue 1: Face away from the cable, rope between the legs
Cue 2: Hinge back letting the rope pull the hips back
Cue 3: Drive the hips through and squeeze the glutes, stand tall
Common faults: Pulling with the arms; Squatting instead of hinging; Leaning back at the top
Progress to: KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2); American KB Swing (G2)
Progress by: Heavier, pause at the top, progress to KB swing
Regress by: Band version, shorter range
Same level swaps: Cable Kickback; Band Pull Through; Cable Pull Through
Joint notes: Very back friendly. A great swing and deadlift regression.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8

Why: Hip flexor strength (especially lifting the knee above 90 degrees) declines with age and affects walking, stairs and tripping. Ben Patrick includes it in ATG Zero.
Cue 1: Sit or lie tall
Cue 2: Lift the knee up without leaning back
Cue 3: Lower slowly
Common faults: Leaning back; Arching the low back; Momentum
Progress to: Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Band resistance, standing, longer holds
Regress by: Smaller range
Same level swaps: Psoas March (Standing); Banded Hip Flexor March; Standing Cable Hip Flexion
Joint notes: Gentle and safe. Hip impingement: keep below pain.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8

Why: Bridges and hip thrusts train the glutes at their strongest point (full hip extension) with almost no spinal load. They are essential for back pain, knee pain, posture, sprinting and golf power, and are safe for nearly everyone. Single leg versions fix imbalances.
Variation notes: Paused version: holding the hardest position removes the bounce and builds strength exactly where people usually fail.
Cue 1: Feet flat, shins vertical at the top
Cue 2: Tuck the ribs down, drive through the heels and squeeze the glutes to lift
Cue 3: Pause at the top without arching the low back, lower slowly
Common faults: Arching the low back instead of extending the hips; Feet too far away (all hamstrings); Pushing through the toes
Progress to: Nordic Curl (Full) (G3); Slider Hamstring Curl (G3); Hamstring Curl (Slider) (G3)
Progress by: Bridge → hip thrust off a bench → load (DB, barbell) → single leg, add pauses or bands
Regress to: Frog Pump (G1); Glute Bridge (G1); Hip Thrust (DB) (G1)
Regress by: Floor bridge, shorter range, isometric hold
Same level swaps: Paused Hip Thrust; Barbell Hip Thrust; Barbell Glute Bridge
Joint notes: Very joint friendly. Use a pad on the hips when loaded. Shoulder elevated versions need a stable bench.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (pause 1 to 2s at the top)

Muscles: Glute medius and minimus, hip stabilisers
Why: The side glutes stop the knee caving and the pelvis dropping when on one leg. Weak glute meds are linked to knee pain, hip pain and back pain. Simple band work fixes it and works brilliantly as a warm up (Squat University, Boyle).
Variation notes: Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
Cue 1: Athletic stance, band around the knees or ankles
Cue 2: Push the knees out, step sideways (or lift the leg) leading with the heel
Cue 3: Stay low and keep the pelvis level
Common faults: Rocking the torso side to side; Feet turning out; Letting the band pull the knees in
Progress to: Cossack Squat (G2); Paused Hip Thrust (G2); Lateral Lunge (DB) (G2)
Progress by: Heavier band, band lower on the leg, side plank abduction
Regress by: Side lying with no band, smaller range
Same level swaps: Clam Shell; Monster Walk; Reverse Clam
Joint notes: Very joint friendly, ideal for hip and knee rehab.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 20 each side

Cue 3: Lower slowly

Cue 3: Return

Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Bigger range
Regress by: Smaller range
Same level swaps: Wall Slides (Supine)
Joint notes: Rehab friendly.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down

Muscles: Calves (gastrocnemius straight knee, soleus bent knee), Achilles
Why: Strong calves protect the knee and Achilles and power walking. Ben Patrick's ATG insists on full range (stretch at the bottom). Bent knee versions train the soleus, critical for running and walking endurance.
Cue 1: Full stretch at the bottom
Cue 2: Rise to the highest point on the big toe
Cue 3: Pause, lower slowly (3s)
Common faults: Bouncing; Rolling to the outside of the foot; Partial range
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Single leg, off a step, add load
Regress by: Two legs, hand support, flat floor
Same level swaps: KOT Calf Raise; Single Leg Calf Raise; Calf Raise (Straight Knee)
Joint notes: Achilles pain: slow heavy calf raises are rehab gold.
Default prescription: 3 x 12 to 20 (slow)

Why: Gentle knee bending range work, used after injury or surgery.
Cue 1: Slide the heel towards the bum slowly
Cue 2: Stop at gentle stretch
Cue 3: Return
Common faults: Forcing; Rushing; Holding breath
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Bigger range
Regress by: Smaller range
Same level swaps: Heel Slides
Joint notes: Rehab friendly.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down

Why: Strong calves protect the knee and Achilles and power walking. Ben Patrick's ATG insists on full range (stretch at the bottom). Bent knee versions train the soleus, critical for running and walking endurance.

Why: A simple, joint friendly way to build quad strength and endurance with zero technique demand. Isometrics can reduce knee pain and are ideal for beginners, seniors and anyone who cannot yet squat through full range. The Swiss ball version lets people practise the squat path with support.
Variation notes: Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
Cue 1: Back flat against the wall, feet hip width and slightly in front
Cue 2: Slide down until the knees are at a pain free angle (aim 90 degrees over time)
Cue 3: Weight through the whole foot, breathe slowly, knees in line with toes
Common faults: Hands pushing on the thighs; Knees caving in; Going too deep too soon and aggravating knees
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Lower the position, hold longer, hold a plate, progress to single leg wall sit or tempo goblet squats
Regress by: Higher position, shorter holds, hands on thighs for the first few sessions
Same level swaps: Wall Sit; Isometric Squat Hold; Swiss Ball Wall Squat
Joint notes: Very knee friendly at higher positions. Adjust depth to stay at or below 3/10 pain. Avoid long holds with breath holding for members with high blood pressure.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 45s holds, rest 60s, about 70% effort
Coach sources: Squat University, Rehab research (isometrics), Ben Patrick

Why: Hamstrings both extend the hip and bend the knee; curls train the knee bending role that RDLs miss. Strong hamstrings protect knees and reduce hamstring strain risk. Nordic curls are among the best researched injury prevention exercises.
Variation notes: Swiss ball adds instability for core control (Paul Chek); keep loads modest.
Cue 1: Lie on your back, heels on the ball/sliders/TRX, lift the hips
Cue 2: Curl the heels towards the bum keeping the hips high
Cue 3: Extend slowly back out (control is the exercise)
Common faults: Hips dropping during the curl; Rushing the lowering; Cramping (start with fewer reps)
Progress to: Single Leg Swiss Ball Curl (G3); Nordic Curl (Full) (G3); Slider Hamstring Curl (G3)
Progress by: Hips stay up throughout, single leg, slower lowering, Nordic progression
Regress to: Swiss Ball Bridge (G1); Frog Pump (G1); Glute Bridge (G1)
Regress by: Hips on the floor curl, eccentric only, double leg
Same level swaps: Swiss Ball Hamstring Curl; TRX Hamstring Curl
Joint notes: Knee friendly. Nordics are demanding: use band assistance and partial range, expect soreness at first.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9

Why: A band behind the knees lets the shins stay vertical while the hips sit back, so the quads work hard with very little compressive stress on the front of the knee. Isometric holds like this are one of the best known tools for calming irritable knees (patellar tendon and kneecap pain) while still loading the quads. A Squat University and physio favourite.
Variation notes: Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
Cue 1: Heavy band behind both knees anchored to the rig, walk back until it is tight
Cue 2: Sit back and down until thighs are around 60 to 90 degrees, shins vertical
Cue 3: Keep chest proud, push knees back into the band and hold
Common faults: Letting the knees drift forward off the band; Holding the breath for the whole set; Going so deep that pain rises above 3/10
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Hold longer (45s), sit deeper, add a weight held at the chest, progress to tempo goblet squats and Poliquin step ups
Regress by: Shorten the hold, sit less deep, lighter band, switch to a wall sit with a higher position
Same level swaps: Spanish Squat (Band)
Joint notes: Knee friendly by design. Often reduces knee pain for several hours afterwards, which makes it a great warm up before squatting for sore knees. Back is upright so low back load is minimal.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 45s holds, rest 60s, about 70% effort (5 x 45s is a classic tendon dose)
Coach sources: Squat University, Ben Patrick (knee resilience), Rehab research (tendon isometrics)

Why: Hamstrings both extend the hip and bend the knee; curls train the knee bending role that RDLs miss. Strong hamstrings protect knees and reduce hamstring strain risk. Nordic curls are among the best researched injury prevention exercises.

Cue 1: Lie on your back, heels on the ball/sliders/TRX, lift the hips
Cue 2: Curl the heels towards the bum keeping the hips high
Cue 3: Extend slowly back out (control is the exercise)
Common faults: Hips dropping during the curl; Rushing the lowering; Cramping (start with fewer reps)
Progress to: Single Leg Slider Curl (G4); Single Leg Box Squat (G4)
Progress by: Hips stay up throughout, single leg, slower lowering, Nordic progression
Regress to: TRX Hamstring Curl (G2); Swiss Ball Hamstring Curl (G2); Hamstring Curl (Swiss Ball) (G2)
Regress by: Hips on the floor curl, eccentric only, double leg
Same level swaps: Slider Hamstring Curl; Nordic Curl (Full); Single Leg Swiss Ball Curl
Joint notes: Knee friendly. Nordics are demanding: use band assistance and partial range, expect soreness at first.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9

Why: First stage quad work for knee pain, after surgery and for replacements. Terminal knee extensions train the last part of straightening the knee, which is often lost.
Variation notes: Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
Cue 1: Tighten the thigh to straighten the knee
Cue 2: Hold 3 to 5s
Cue 3: Lower slowly
Common faults: Rushing; Bent knee in straight leg raise; Lifting too high
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Add ankle weight, band
Regress by: No load
Same level swaps: Terminal Knee Extension (Band); Short Arc Quad; Straight Leg Raise
Joint notes: Rehab friendly.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 x 10 to 15, 3s holds

Why: The box sets a consistent, safe depth and teaches people to sit back and control the descent. It is the best teaching squat for beginners and painful knees and, with a barbell or SSB, a classic DeFranco/Westside strength builder.
Variation notes: Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
Cue 1: Box at a height where the spine stays neutral
Cue 2: Sit back and down with control, touch the box lightly (don't crash)
Cue 3: Stay braced, drive up through the whole foot
Common faults: Plonking down and relaxing on the box; Rocking back to get up; Knees caving as they stand
Progress to: Barbell Box Squat (G2); Banded Barbell Box Squat (G2)
Progress by: Lower the box, add load (goblet then SSB/barbell), pause on the box without relaxing, remove the box
Regress by: Raise the box, TRX assisted box squat, sit to stand
Same level swaps: Box Squat; Goblet Box Squat
Joint notes: Excellent for knee pain and older members: adjust height to the pain free range. Lower the box as mobility and control improve.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Muscles: Quads, glutes, adductors, upper back, core
Why: Holding the weight at the chest counterbalances the body, so people naturally squat more upright and deeper with better form. Dan John and Squat University both use it as THE teaching squat, and it is strong enough to stay useful for years. Fits groups perfectly because load scales from a 4kg KB to a 40kg+ DB.
Variation notes: Combination move: trains two qualities at once, efficient for HYBRID and BURN; keep technique of both parts clean before speeding up.
Cue 1: Hold the bell tight to the chest, elbows pointing down
Cue 2: Push the knees out and sit between the hips, chest proud
Cue 3: Drive up through the whole foot, squeeze the glutes at the top
Common faults: Rounding the upper back and letting the weight pull you forward; Heels lifting; Knees caving inward on the way up
Progress to: Paused Goblet Squat (G3); 1.5 Rep Goblet Squat (G3)
Progress by: Add load, tempo (4-1-1-0), pause at the bottom, 1.5 reps, move to double KB front squat or SSB squat
Regress to: Goblet Box Squat (G1); Box Squat (G1); TRX Assisted Squat (G1)
Regress by: Goblet squat to a box, TRX assisted squat, lighter bell
Same level swaps: Goblet Squat (KB); Goblet Squat (DB); Tempo Goblet Squat
Joint notes: Knee and back friendly. Heels elevated version helps stiff ankles. Use a box for depth control with knee pain. Upper back can fatigue first as loads get heavy.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
Coach sources: Dan John, Squat University, Cosgrove, Boyle

Muscles: Heart and lungs, legs (bike/rower), upper body (ski/rower)
Why: The bike, rower and ski erg give big conditioning with no impact, and every level can work at their own intensity. Zone 2 builds the aerobic base (Attia); short sprints suit menopause and fat loss (Sims, Cosgrove hierarchy). Backward walking (treadmill or sled) is Ben Patrick's knee warm up.
Cue 1: Bike: push and pull with arms and legs, steady cadence
Cue 2: Rower: legs, body, arms; then arms, body, legs
Cue 3: Ski: hinge and pull down, drive the hips
Common faults: Rowing with the arms first; Hunched posture; Going out too hard in intervals
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Longer work, shorter rest, higher watts/calories, more rounds
Regress by: Easier pace, shorter intervals, more rest
Same level swaps: Tabata Bike; Bike (Easy); Bike Erg Intervals
Joint notes: Low impact. Rower and ski: watch low back flexion. Treadmill sprints involve impact.
Default prescription: Intervals: e.g. 6 to 10 x 15 to 30s hard / 60 to 90s easy, or 20 to 40 min steady (zone 2)
Coach sources: Attia (zone 2, VO2), Cosgrove (intervals), Stacy Sims (sprints), Ben Patrick (backward walking)

Why: Ben Patrick's number one knee tool: walking backwards loads the quads with the knee travelling over the toes, floods the knee with blood and is nearly impossible to overdo.
Cue 1: Lean back slightly against the sled (or hold the treadmill rails)
Cue 2: Small steps, push through the front of the foot
Cue 3: Knees travel over the toes
Common faults: Big steps; Standing tall; Too heavy
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Heavier, longer
Regress by: Lighter, treadmill flat
Same level swaps: Sled Drag Backwards; Sled Drag (Backwards); Backwards Walking (Treadmill Incline)
Joint notes: Knee pain staple. Very safe.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 min warm up, or 4 to 6 x 20m

Why: Foam rolling reduces the sensation of stiffness and prepares tissues for movement (Cosgrove template step 1). Short, targeted, before the session.
Cue 1: Roll slowly
Cue 2: Pause on tender spots and breathe
Cue 3: 30 to 60s per area
Common faults: Rolling on the low back; Too long; Rolling acute injuries
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Firmer tools
Regress by: Softer roller
Same level swaps: Foam Roll Quads; Foam Roll Calves; Foam Roll Thoracic Spine
Joint notes: Avoid rolling directly on bones, varicose veins or acute injuries.
Default prescription: 30 to 60s per area

Why: Controlled lowering from a step builds knee control and eccentric quad strength, the exact quality needed for walking downstairs. Also a key screening test for knee valgus and hip control.
Cue 1: Stand on a box, other leg hanging off the front or side
Cue 2: Lower slowly by bending the standing knee, hips back slightly
Cue 3: Tap the heel lightly and return without pushing off the floor
Common faults: Knee diving in; Hip dropping on the free side; Crashing down to the floor
Progress to: Pistol Squat (G3); Skater Squat (G3); Shrimp Squat (G3)
Progress by: Higher box, hold weight, slower lowering
Regress to: Patrick Step (G1); Poliquin Step Up (G1); Petersen Step Up (G1)
Regress by: Lower box, hand support, Poliquin step up
Same level swaps: Low Box Step Down; Lateral Step Down; Heel Tap Step Down
Joint notes: Excellent for knee rehab when the box is low. Raise the height as control improves.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 8 to 12 each leg, 3s lowering

Muscles: Target muscles and joints vary (named in the exercise)
Why: Static and gentle mobility work restores range lost from sitting and ageing. Best used where a screen shows a restriction (Squat University: screen, correct, retest), and to cool down. McKenzie press ups and extension work often relieve disc type back pain; flexion stretches often suit stenosis type pain: individualise.
Cue 1: Get into position slowly
Cue 2: Breathe out to relax into range, no bouncing
Cue 3: Hold 30 to 60s or do slow reps
Common faults: Forcing painful range; Holding the breath; Stretching instead of strengthening when stability is the issue
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Longer holds, deeper range, add loaded stretching
Regress by: Smaller range, supported versions
Same level swaps: Frog Stretch; Couch Stretch; Elephant Walk
Joint notes: Gentle and safe. Stop if symptoms travel down the leg. Osteoporosis: avoid loaded flexion stretches.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
Coach sources: Squat University, DeFranco (Limber 11), Ben Patrick (couch stretch), McGill

Why: Stiff ankles cause heels lifting, knees caving and forward lean in squats, and pain further up the chain (joint by joint). The knee to wall test is the screen; rocks and banded mobs are the fix (Squat University).
Cue 1: Half kneeling, foot about 10cm from the wall
Cue 2: Drive the knee forward over the toes keeping the heel down
Cue 3: Rock in and out
Common faults: Heel lifting; Knee caving inward; Forcing
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Further from the wall, band, load
Regress by: Closer to the wall
Same level swaps: Banded Ankle Mobility; Ankle Rocks (Knee to Wall)
Joint notes: Universally safe.
Default prescription: 2 x 10 to 15 rocks each side

Why: The entry point of the single leg ladder. A static split stance gives a stable base, so people learn to load one leg at a time safely. It builds balance, fixes imbalances and is far easier on the back than heavy bilateral squats. Front foot elevated adds knee travel (ATG style); cable and landmine versions add stability.
Variation notes: Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
Cue 1: Long split stance, both feet pointing forward, hip width apart
Cue 2: Lower the back knee straight down towards the floor
Cue 3: Push through the front foot to stand, keep the torso tall
Common faults: Stance too narrow (tightrope), losing balance; Front heel lifting; Lunging forward instead of dropping down
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); Split Squat (DB) (G2)
Progress by: Add load, elevate the front foot (ATG style), then elevate the back foot (RFESS)
Regress by: TRX or rig assisted split squat, shorter range, isometric split squat hold
Same level swaps: Split Squat (Supported); Split Squat (Bodyweight); TRX Assisted Split Squat
Joint notes: Knee friendly when depth is controlled. Use a pad under the back knee. Hold a support for balance in seniors.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)
Coach sources: Boyle, Squat University, Ben Patrick (front foot elevated)

Categories: REHAB: KNEE; MOBILITY AND WARM UP

Cue 3: Push through the front foot to stand, keep the torso tall

Progress to: Barbell Split Squat (G3); Band Resisted Split Squat (G3); Offset Single Arm Split Squat (G3)

Regress to: Split Squat (Supported) (G1); Split Squat (Bodyweight) (G1); TRX Assisted Split Squat (G1)
Regress by: TRX or rig assisted split squat, shorter range, isometric split squat hold

Muscles: Quads (rectus femoris in a lengthened position), hip flexors
Why: Trains the quads with the knees travelling far over the toes and the hips extended. Builds strength in the end range of knee bending, which Ben Patrick uses to bulletproof knees. Assisted versions are surprisingly accessible.
Variation notes: Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress). Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
Cue 1: Hold a post or TRX for support
Cue 2: Rise onto the toes, push the knees forward and lean the body back as one straight line from knee to shoulder
Cue 3: Lower only as far as pain free, drive back up through the quads
Common faults: Bending at the hips (turns it into a normal squat); Dropping too deep too early; Letting go of the support before ready
Progress to: Single Leg Mini Squat (G3); Reverse Lunge (Slider) (G3); Hamstring Curl (Slider) (G3)
Progress by: Increase range, reduce hand assistance, add a plate at the chest, progress towards reverse Nordic
Regress to: Heel Slides (G1); Glute Bridge (G1); Couch Stretch (G1)
Regress by: Short range only, more hand support, swap to Spanish squat or heels elevated goblet squat
Same level swaps: Sissy Squat (Assisted); Reverse Nordic (Assisted)
Joint notes: Earn it. Start short range with hand support. Avoid with acute knee pain, recent knee surgery or knee replacements unless cleared.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 6 to 12 reps, slow lowering, hand support

Why: Stepping backwards keeps the shin more vertical, so it is far kinder to the knees than forward lunges while still training single leg strength and balance. The default lunge at Optimal. Deficit and slider versions increase range and control.
Variation notes: Sliders add a friction based eccentric control challenge.
Cue 1: Stand tall, step one foot back
Cue 2: Drop the back knee towards the floor, front shin fairly vertical
Cue 3: Drive through the front heel to stand back up
Common faults: Stepping too short; Front knee collapsing; Leaning forward and rounding
Progress to: Single Leg Box Squat (G4)
Progress by: Add load, deficit (front foot on a plate), knee drive at the top, barbell/landmine
Regress to: SSB Reverse Lunge (G2); Reverse Lunge (DB) (G2); Cable Reverse Lunge (G2)
Regress by: Split squat (static), hand support, shorter range
Same level swaps: Slider Reverse Lunge; Deficit Reverse Lunge; Barbell Reverse Lunge
Joint notes: Most knee friendly lunge. Use a pad and hand support for beginners.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)

Muscles: Whole lower body, tendons, nervous system
Why: Jumps and hops train power, tendon stiffness and bone (impact is a key bone stimulus in LIFTMOR). Landings (snap downs, drop squats, jump and stick) teach the body to absorb force, the foundation of injury prevention. Progress carefully: landing before jumping, low before high, two legs before one.
Cue 1: Land softly and quietly, hips back, knees over toes
Cue 2: Stick the landing for a second before the next rep
Cue 3: Quality over quantity: stop when height or control drops
Common faults: Landing stiff legged or with knees caving; Too many reps (plyos are not cardio); Progressing too fast
Progress to: A Skip (G3); Box Jump (G3); Bounding (G3)
Progress by: Landings → small jumps → box jumps → broad jumps → single leg hops → depth jumps
Regress to: Heel Slides (G1); Glute Bridge (G1); Couch Stretch (G1)
Regress by: Snap downs/drop squat and stick, step ups, sled push, med ball throws
Same level swaps: Snap Downs; Drop Squat; Drop Squat and Stick
Cautions: Knee, Low back, Osteoporosis/osteopenia, Pelvic floor
Joint notes: IMPACT: excluded from Optimal GROUP sessions (no jumping rule). Teams only after screening. Avoid with pelvic floor symptoms, osteoporosis with fracture history, joint replacements, acute knee/Achilles pain.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 sets x 3 to 6 reps, full recovery (60 to 120s), stop when speed drops; 2 to 3 sessions/week max, low total contacts (20 to 60)
Group alternative: Group swap (no jumping): sled push, fast step ups, med ball chest pass or slam, KB swing, fast sit to stand
Coach sources: Gambetta, DeFranco (dynamic effort), LIFTMOR research (impact for bone)

Muscles: Quads, glutes, adductors, balance and foot control
Why: Single leg squats are the top of Mike Boyle's single leg ladder: maximum leg strength with minimal spinal load, and they expose left/right imbalances. Box versions control depth so they are accessible far earlier than a full pistol.
Cue 1: Stand on one leg, other leg held forward (pistol) or behind (skater/shrimp)
Cue 2: Sit back and down slowly to the box or depth target, knee over the middle of the foot
Cue 3: Drive up through the whole foot without the knee caving
Common faults: Knee diving inward; Collapsing onto the box; Heel lifting
Progress to: Single Leg Box Squat (G4); Single Leg Squat to Bench (G4)
Progress by: Lower the box, remove support, add a light counterweight held forward, then load
Regress to: Low Box Step Down (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Forward Step Down (G2)
Regress by: Higher box, TRX assisted, step downs, split squat
Same level swaps: Pistol Squat; Skater Squat; Shrimp Squat
Joint notes: Demanding on the knee. Use a box and TRX support first. Not for acute knee pain or early post surgery.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 5 to 8 each leg, slow lowering

Muscles: Whole lower body, tendons, nervous system
Why: Jumps and hops train power, tendon stiffness and bone (impact is a key bone stimulus in LIFTMOR). Landings (snap downs, drop squats, jump and stick) teach the body to absorb force, the foundation of injury prevention. Progress carefully: landing before jumping, low before high, two legs before one.
Cue 1: Land softly and quietly, hips back, knees over toes
Cue 2: Stick the landing for a second before the next rep
Cue 3: Quality over quantity: stop when height or control drops
Common faults: Landing stiff legged or with knees caving; Too many reps (plyos are not cardio); Progressing too fast
Progress to: A Skip (G3); Box Jump (G3); Bounding (G3)
Progress by: Landings → small jumps → box jumps → broad jumps → single leg hops → depth jumps
Regress to: Heel Slides (G1); Glute Bridge (G1); Couch Stretch (G1)
Regress by: Snap downs/drop squat and stick, step ups, sled push, med ball throws
Same level swaps: Snap Downs; Drop Squat; Pogo Hops (Low)
Cautions: Knee, Low back, Osteoporosis/osteopenia, Pelvic floor
Joint notes: IMPACT: excluded from Optimal GROUP sessions (no jumping rule). Teams only after screening. Avoid with pelvic floor symptoms, osteoporosis with fracture history, joint replacements, acute knee/Achilles pain.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 sets x 3 to 6 reps, full recovery (60 to 120s), stop when speed drops; 2 to 3 sessions/week max, low total contacts (20 to 60)
Coach sources: Gambetta, DeFranco (dynamic effort), LIFTMOR research (impact for bone)

Why: The most important real life squat: getting up from a chair or toilet. A key longevity skill and a core test for seniors (30 second sit to stand). Done fast on the way up, it trains power, which declines faster than strength with age.
Cue 1: Sit tall on a box or chair, feet slightly back under the knees
Cue 2: Lean the chest forward, push the floor away and stand up tall
Cue 3: Sit back down slowly with control, don't flop
Common faults: Using the hands to push off; Feet too far forward; Collapsing back down onto the seat
Progress to: Cyclist Squat (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2)
Progress by: Lower the box, hold a weight at the chest, stand up as fast as possible (power), single leg sit to stand
Regress by: Raise the seat, use hands on thighs or a TRX for help, reduce reps
Same level swaps: Fast Sit to Stand (Power); Squat to Box Stand Up (Bodyweight)
Joint notes: Suitable for almost everyone. Raise the seat height for painful knees or hips. Single leg version needs good knee control.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps (or max reps in 30s for testing), stand up fast, lower slowly
Coach sources: Seniors research (functional testing), Gambetta (fundamental movement), Attia (centenarian decathlon)

Why: Breathing is the foundation of bracing (Chek: breathing first). Crocodile and 90/90 breathing teach 360 degree breathing, calm the nervous system and help back pain and pelvic floor function.
Cue 1: Lie in position, hands on the lower ribs
Cue 2: Breathe in through the nose expanding 360 degrees (belly, sides, back)
Cue 3: Exhale slowly fully, feeling the ribs drop
Common faults: Chest and shoulder breathing; Arching the back; Rushing
Progress to: Side Plank (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2); Bear Plank Hold (G2)
Progress by: Add movement (dead bug with breathing)
Regress by: Shorter sets
Same level swaps: Pelvic Tilt; 90/90 Breathing; Pelvic Tilt (Supine)
Joint notes: Universally safe. Great on RED readiness days.
Default prescription: 5 to 10 slow breaths

Pattern: Core: anti extension + anti rotation (Swiss ball)
Why: McGill's favourite advanced core drill: forearms on a Swiss ball making small circles while the body stays rigid.
Cue 1: Forearms on the ball, plank position
Cue 2: Draw small circles with the elbows
Cue 3: Keep the hips and back still
Common faults: Hips sagging; Big circles; Holding the breath
Progress by: Bigger circles, feet narrower
Regress to: Side Plank (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2); Bear Plank Hold (G2)
Regress by: Swiss ball plank hold
Same level swaps: Swiss Ball Stir the Pot; Stir the Pot (Swiss Ball)
Joint notes: Safe for backs when form is held. Shoulder pain: reduce range.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 x 5 to 10 circles each way

Why: Rollouts and body saws are advanced anti extension: the further the arms reach, the harder the core works to stop the back arching.
Variation notes: Swiss ball adds instability for core control (Paul Chek); keep loads modest. Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
Cue 1: Kneeling or plank, ribs down, glutes tight
Cue 2: Roll or slide out only as far as you can keep the back flat
Cue 3: Pull back using the abs and lats
Common faults: Low back sagging; Hips piking first; Going too far too soon
Progress to: Swiss Ball Rollout (G4); Barbell Rollout (G4); Slider Body Saw (G4)
Progress by: Longer range, from feet
Regress to: Plank Saw (G2); RKC Plank (G2); Front Plank (G2)
Regress by: Swiss ball rollout short range, plank
Same level swaps: TRX Fallout; TRX Body Saw; Ab Wheel Rollout (Kneeling)
Joint notes: Can strain the low back if overreached. Shoulder pain: limit range.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 6 to 10 reps each side (or 20 to 40s), slow and controlled

Why: Strengthens the back extensors and glutes, improving posture and back resilience. Reverse hypers decompress the spine as they train. Extend to neutral only: the goal is a strong, straight spine, not arching.
Variation notes: Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
Cue 1: Hinge at the hips, keep the spine long
Cue 2: Lift to a straight line from head to heels using the glutes
Cue 3: Lower with control
Common faults: Hyperextending at the top; Swinging/using momentum; Rounding heavily at the bottom under load
Progress to: Prone Cobra (Chek) (G2); Reverse Hyper (Bench) (G2); Superman (Alternating) (G2)
Progress by: Hold a plate, single leg, pause at the top
Regress by: Superman, bird dog, shorter range
Same level swaps: 45 Degree Back Extension (Bodyweight)
Joint notes: Good for most back pain when kept to neutral. Avoid loaded flexion at the bottom for osteoporosis.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
Coach sources: DeFranco (reverse hyper), McGill, Paul Chek (prone cobra)

Categories: REHAB: LOWER BACK; MOBILITY AND WARM UP
Why: Gentle spinal mobility for back care and warm ups. Extension drills (prone lying, McKenzie press ups) often ease disc type back pain; flexion drills (knee to chest, child's pose) often ease stiffness and stenosis type pain. Find the direction that helps the individual (McGill: find the pain triggers) and use it.
Cue 1: Move slowly through comfortable range
Cue 2: Breathe out into the end range
Cue 3: Stop if symptoms travel down a leg
Common faults: Forcing range; Holding the breath; Bouncing
Progress to: Side Plank (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2); Bear Plank Hold (G2)
Progress by: Bigger range, add breathing holds
Regress by: Smaller range
Same level swaps: Child's Pose; Supine Twist; Lying Knee Drops
Joint notes: Generally very safe. Osteoporosis: avoid repeated or loaded spinal flexion. Pain spreading into a leg: stop and refer.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down

Muscles: Target muscles and joints vary (named in the exercise)
Why: Static and gentle mobility work restores range lost from sitting and ageing. Best used where a screen shows a restriction (Squat University: screen, correct, retest), and to cool down. McKenzie press ups and extension work often relieve disc type back pain; flexion stretches often suit stenosis type pain: individualise.
Cue 1: Get into position slowly
Cue 2: Breathe out to relax into range, no bouncing
Cue 3: Hold 30 to 60s or do slow reps
Common faults: Forcing painful range; Holding the breath; Stretching instead of strengthening when stability is the issue
Progress to: Side Plank (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2); Bear Plank Hold (G2)
Progress by: Longer holds, deeper range, add loaded stretching
Regress by: Smaller range, supported versions
Same level swaps: Frog Stretch; Couch Stretch; Elephant Walk
Joint notes: Gentle and safe. Stop if symptoms travel down the leg. Osteoporosis: avoid loaded flexion stretches.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
Coach sources: Squat University, DeFranco (Limber 11), Ben Patrick (couch stretch), McGill

Why: Foam rolling reduces the sensation of stiffness and prepares tissues for movement (Cosgrove template step 1). Short, targeted, before the session.
Cue 1: Roll slowly
Cue 2: Pause on tender spots and breathe
Cue 3: 30 to 60s per area
Common faults: Rolling on the low back; Too long; Rolling acute injuries
Progress to: Side Plank (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2); Bear Plank Hold (G2)
Progress by: Firmer tools
Regress by: Softer roller
Same level swaps: Foam Roll Quads; Foam Roll Calves; Patellar Mobilisation
Joint notes: Avoid rolling directly on bones, varicose veins or acute injuries.
Default prescription: 30 to 60s per area

Why: Keeps the low back flat while the arms and legs move: anti extension control and coordination. Safe for almost everyone and the foundation of bracing (McGill, Chek).
Cue 1: Back flat, ribs down, knees and arms up
Cue 2: Slowly extend the opposite arm and leg while breathing out
Cue 3: Return and swap without the back arching
Common faults: Low back lifting; Moving fast; Holding the breath
Progress to: Plank Saw (G2); RKC Plank (G2); Front Plank (G2)
Progress by: Straighter legs, band resisted, KB pullover, slower
Regress by: Heel taps, arms only
Same level swaps: Dead Bug; Dead Bug Heel Taps; Dead Bug Bridge Hold
Joint notes: Back pain friendly. Pelvic floor friendly.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 6 to 10 reps each side (or 20 to 40s), slow and controlled

Why: The plank trains the core to resist extension. Useful foundation, part of the Optimal screen (30s kneeling → full plank → plank with full tension). Long lever and RKC versions dramatically increase difficulty without longer holds.
Variation notes: Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
Cue 1: Elbows under shoulders, straight line head to heels
Cue 2: Squeeze glutes, pull the ribs down, push the floor away
Cue 3: Breathe, hold with full tension
Common faults: Sagging hips; Bum in the air; Holding for minutes with poor form
Progress to: Single Arm Plank (G3); Long Lever Plank (G3)
Progress by: Long lever, RKC plank, leg lift, body saw
Regress to: Dead Bug (G1); Plank on Knees (G1); Dead Bug Heel Taps (G1)
Regress by: Plank on knees, incline plank on a bench
Same level swaps: Plank Saw; RKC Plank; Front Plank
Joint notes: Shoulder or wrist pain: dead bug or Pallof press instead. Prefer 20 to 30s high tension holds over long sloppy ones.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 20 to 40s (high tension)

Muscles: Heart and lungs, legs (bike/rower), upper body (ski/rower)
Why: The bike, rower and ski erg give big conditioning with no impact, and every level can work at their own intensity. Zone 2 builds the aerobic base (Attia); short sprints suit menopause and fat loss (Sims, Cosgrove hierarchy). Backward walking (treadmill or sled) is Ben Patrick's knee warm up.
Cue 1: Bike: push and pull with arms and legs, steady cadence
Cue 2: Rower: legs, body, arms; then arms, body, legs
Cue 3: Ski: hinge and pull down, drive the hips
Common faults: Rowing with the arms first; Hunched posture; Going out too hard in intervals
Progress to: Side Plank (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2); Bear Plank Hold (G2)
Progress by: Longer work, shorter rest, higher watts/calories, more rounds
Regress by: Easier pace, shorter intervals, more rest
Same level swaps: Treadmill Incline Walk; Incline Walk (Treadmill); Rower 500m
Joint notes: Low impact. Rower and ski: watch low back flexion. Treadmill sprints involve impact.
Default prescription: Intervals: e.g. 6 to 10 x 15 to 30s hard / 60 to 90s easy, or 20 to 40 min steady (zone 2)
Coach sources: Attia (zone 2, VO2), Cosgrove (intervals), Stacy Sims (sprints), Ben Patrick (backward walking)

Why: Bridges and hip thrusts train the glutes at their strongest point (full hip extension) with almost no spinal load. They are essential for back pain, knee pain, posture, sprinting and golf power, and are safe for nearly everyone. Single leg versions fix imbalances.
Cue 1: Feet flat, shins vertical at the top
Cue 2: Tuck the ribs down, drive through the heels and squeeze the glutes to lift
Cue 3: Pause at the top without arching the low back, lower slowly
Common faults: Arching the low back instead of extending the hips; Feet too far away (all hamstrings); Pushing through the toes
Progress to: Paused Hip Thrust (G2); Barbell Hip Thrust (G2); Hip Thrust (Paused) (G2)
Progress by: Bridge → hip thrust off a bench → load (DB, barbell) → single leg, add pauses or bands
Regress by: Floor bridge, shorter range, isometric hold
Same level swaps: Frog Pump; Glute Bridge; Hip Thrust (DB)
Joint notes: Very joint friendly. Use a pad on the hips when loaded. Shoulder elevated versions need a stable bench.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (pause 1 to 2s at the top)

Default prescription: Intervals: e.g. 6 to 10 x 15 to 30s hard / 60 to 90s easy, or 20 to 40 min steady (zone 2)
Coach sources: Attia (zone 2, VO2), Cosgrove (intervals), Stacy Sims (sprints), Ben Patrick (backward walking)

Muscles: Heart and lungs, legs (bike/rower), upper body (ski/rower)
Why: The bike, rower and ski erg give big conditioning with no impact, and every level can work at their own intensity. Zone 2 builds the aerobic base (Attia); short sprints suit menopause and fat loss (Sims, Cosgrove hierarchy). Backward walking (treadmill or sled) is Ben Patrick's knee warm up.
Cue 1: Bike: push and pull with arms and legs, steady cadence
Cue 2: Rower: legs, body, arms; then arms, body, legs
Cue 3: Ski: hinge and pull down, drive the hips
Common faults: Rowing with the arms first; Hunched posture; Going out too hard in intervals
Progress to: Side Plank (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2); Bear Plank Hold (G2)
Progress by: Longer work, shorter rest, higher watts/calories, more rounds
Regress by: Easier pace, shorter intervals, more rest
Same level swaps: Tabata Bike; Bike Erg Intervals; Assault Bike Sprint
Joint notes: Low impact. Rower and ski: watch low back flexion. Treadmill sprints involve impact.
Default prescription: Intervals: e.g. 6 to 10 x 15 to 30s hard / 60 to 90s easy, or 20 to 40 min steady (zone 2)
Coach sources: Attia (zone 2, VO2), Cosgrove (intervals), Stacy Sims (sprints), Ben Patrick (backward walking)

Why: Teaches people to move at the hips not the spine. The dowel gives instant feedback (head, upper back and tailbone stay in contact). Every hinge exercise depends on this skill, so McGill and Squat University teach it first.
Cue 1: Dowel along the spine touching head, upper back and tailbone
Cue 2: Soft knees, push the hips back as if closing a car door with your bum
Cue 3: Hinge until you feel the hamstrings, keep all three contact points, stand back up
Common faults: Losing the dowel contact at the low back; Bending the knees into a squat; Looking up and cranking the neck
Progress to: Double KB Deadlift (G2); Single Arm Cable Pull Through (G2)
Progress by: Hold a KB at the chest, progress to KB deadlift from blocks
Regress by: Hinge to a wall (bum touches the wall) with a smaller range
Same level swaps: KB Deadlift; DB Deadlift; Donkey Kick
Joint notes: Ideal for back pain members. No load, no risk.
Default prescription: 2 sets x 8 to 10 slow reps (warm up)

Why: Cable/band pull throughs teach the hip hinge with the load pulling from behind, so people naturally sit the hips back and finish with the glutes. Kickbacks and quadruped hip extensions isolate the glutes for activation and rehab.
Variation notes: Cable: constant tension through the whole range with smooth, joint friendly resistance. Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
Cue 1: Face away from the cable, rope between the legs
Cue 2: Hinge back letting the rope pull the hips back
Cue 3: Drive the hips through and squeeze the glutes, stand tall
Common faults: Pulling with the arms; Squatting instead of hinging; Leaning back at the top
Progress to: Single Arm Cable Pull Through (G2); KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2)
Progress by: Heavier, pause at the top, progress to KB swing
Regress by: Band version, shorter range
Same level swaps: Cable Kickback; Band Pull Through; Cable Pull Through
Joint notes: Very back friendly. A great swing and deadlift regression.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8

Why: The safest way to teach lifting from the floor. Picking things up is a life skill (Primal Pattern 'bend'). Raising the bell on blocks reduces range for beginners and back pain; suitcase versions add anti lateral flexion.
Cue 1: Bell between the feet (or beside for suitcase), hinge down with a flat back
Cue 2: Grip, pull the shoulders down, brace
Cue 3: Push the floor away and stand tall, squeeze the glutes
Common faults: Squatting down too low; Rounding to reach the bell; Leaning back at the top
Progress to: KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2); American KB Swing (G2)
Progress by: Heavier bell, double KB, lower to the floor, progress to RDL, swing and trap bar
Regress by: Bell on a block/step, hinge drill
Same level swaps: KB Deadlift; Sumo KB Deadlift; Elevated KB Deadlift
Joint notes: Very back friendly. Elevate the bell on a step for limited hip mobility or back history.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Why: One side loading turns a carry into an anti lateral flexion core exercise: you must stop the body leaning. McGill calls the suitcase carry one of the best core exercises.
Variation notes: One sided loading adds an anti rotation / anti lateral flexion core challenge and exposes left/right differences.
Cue 1: Weight in one hand, stand tall, shoulders level
Cue 2: Walk slowly without leaning towards or away from the weight
Cue 3: Swap hands
Common faults: Leaning; Shrugging the loaded side; Rushing
Progress to: Uneven Front Rack Carry (G3); Stir the Pot (G3); Supine Hollow Hold (Tuck) (G3)
Progress by: Heavier, march with high knees, longer
Regress to: Farmer's Carry (G1); Farmer's Carry March (G1); Farmer's Hold (Static) (G1)
Regress by: Lighter, static hold
Same level swaps: Suitcase Hold; Suitcase March; Cross Body Carry
Joint notes: Back pain friendly.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 40m (or 30 to 45s), rest 60 to 90s each side

Why: Dan John says loaded carries change lives. Picking up heavy things and walking trains grip (a strong longevity predictor), posture, core and conditioning all at once, with low technical demand and low injury risk. Every member, every week.
Cue 1: Deadlift the weights up properly
Cue 2: Stand tall, shoulders down, walk with short controlled steps
Cue 3: Breathe and keep the ribs down
Common faults: Shrugging; Leaning forward or side to side; Fast sloppy steps
Progress to: Suitcase Hold (G2); Suitcase March (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2)
Progress by: Heavier, longer, on the toes, with steps/obstacles; Dan John standard: bodyweight total for men
Regress by: Lighter, shorter, static hold
Same level swaps: Farmer's Carry March; Farmer's Hold (Static); Farmer's Carry on Toes
Joint notes: Very safe. Pick up and put down with a good hinge. Grip limited members: straps are fine to train the rest.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 x 20 to 40m (or 30 to 45s), rest 60 to 90s

Muscles: Glute medius and minimus, hip stabilisers
Why: The side glutes stop the knee caving and the pelvis dropping when on one leg. Weak glute meds are linked to knee pain, hip pain and back pain. Simple band work fixes it and works brilliantly as a warm up (Squat University, Boyle).
Cue 1: Athletic stance, band around the knees or ankles
Cue 2: Push the knees out, step sideways (or lift the leg) leading with the heel
Cue 3: Stay low and keep the pelvis level
Common faults: Rocking the torso side to side; Feet turning out; Letting the band pull the knees in
Progress to: Cossack Squat (G2); Paused Hip Thrust (G2); Lateral Lunge (DB) (G2)
Progress by: Heavier band, band lower on the leg, side plank abduction
Regress by: Side lying with no band, smaller range
Same level swaps: Clam Shell; Monster Walk; Reverse Clam
Joint notes: Very joint friendly, ideal for hip and knee rehab.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 20 each side

Why: The core's main job is to stop unwanted movement. The Pallof press resists the cable pulling you round, training the anti rotation strength that protects the back and transfers force in golf, tennis and lifting (McGill, Boyle, Cosgrove).
Cue 1: Side on to the cable at chest height, brace
Cue 2: Press the handle straight out from the chest and hold 2s
Cue 3: Don't let the hands or hips rotate, return to the chest
Common faults: Rotating towards the cable; Leaning away; Holding the breath
Progress to: Band Woodchop (G2); Cable Lift with Step (G2); Half Kneeling Cable Chop (G2)
Progress by: Tall kneeling → half kneeling → split → standing → walkouts, add overhead reach, heavier
Regress by: Lighter band, closer to the anchor, iso hold
Same level swaps: Pallof Walkout; Pallof Hold Iso; Pallof Press Lunge
Joint notes: Excellent for back pain. Half kneeling reduces hip involvement and isolates the core.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 6 to 10 reps each side (or 20 to 40s), slow and controlled

Why: A gymnastic anti extension hold. Harder than a dead bug.
Cue 1: Low back pressed down
Cue 2: Arms and legs extended low
Cue 3: Hold
Common faults: Back arching; Holding breath; Neck strain
Progress by: Longer levers, rocks
Regress to: Side Plank (G2); Suitcase Carry (G2); Bear Plank Hold (G2)
Regress by: Tuck hold, dead bug
Same level swaps: Hollow Body Hold; Hollow Body Rock
Joint notes: Can strain the low back if form is lost. Tuck the knees to regress.
Default prescription: 3 x 15 to 30s

Why: Dynamic drills raise temperature, take joints through range and rehearse patterns (RAMP warm up). The World's Greatest Stretch hits hip flexors, hamstrings, adductors and T spine in one move. 40+ members need a full 8 to 10 minute warm up every session.
Cue 1: Move through big comfortable ranges
Cue 2: Increase range each rep
Cue 3: Breathe and stay controlled
Common faults: Rushing; Bouncing into range; Skipping the warm up
Progress to: Bear Crawl (G2); Quadruped Thoracic Rotation (G2); Spiderman Lunge with Rotation (G2)
Progress by: Bigger range, add reaches
Regress by: Smaller range, hand support
Same level swaps: A March; Inchworm; Crab Reach
Joint notes: Safe for almost everyone.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 x 5 to 10 each side (or 20 to 30m)

Muscles: Quads, glutes, upper back, shoulders, core
Why: The overhead squat exposes stiffness at the ankles, hips, T spine and shoulders all at once, which is why Squat University and the FMS use it as a screen. With a dowel it is an excellent mobility drill; loaded it is a high skill G4 lift.

Cue 2: Sit down between the hips with the chest proud
Cue 3: Keep the bar over the middle of the foot throughout
Common faults: Arms drifting forward; Lower back rounding at the bottom; Heels lifting
Progress to: Barbell Overhead Squat (G4)
Progress by: Dowel → light DB/plate → barbell overhead squat
Regress to: Bear Crawl (G2); Quadruped Thoracic Rotation (G2); Spiderman Lunge with Rotation (G2)
Regress by: Dowel only, squat to a box, heels elevated, arms in a Y position
Same level swaps: DB Overhead Squat
Joint notes: Shoulder demanding: avoid loading with shoulder pain or impingement. Use a dowel as a warm up screen instead.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 5 to 8 reps, light, slow

Why: Gentle spinal mobility for back care and warm ups. Extension drills (prone lying, McKenzie press ups) often ease disc type back pain; flexion drills (knee to chest, child's pose) often ease stiffness and stenosis type pain. Find the direction that helps the individual (McGill: find the pain triggers) and use it.
Cue 1: Move slowly through comfortable range
Cue 2: Breathe out into the end range
Cue 3: Stop if symptoms travel down a leg
Common faults: Forcing range; Holding the breath; Bouncing
Progress to: Bear Crawl (G2); Quadruped Thoracic Rotation (G2); Spiderman Lunge with Rotation (G2)
Progress by: Bigger range, add breathing holds
Regress by: Smaller range
Same level swaps: Cat Cow; Child's Pose; Supine Twist
Joint notes: Generally very safe. Osteoporosis: avoid repeated or loaded spinal flexion. Pain spreading into a leg: stop and refer.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down

Muscles: Thoracic spine rotation and extension, lats, pecs
Why: The upper back should move; the low back should be stable (joint by joint). Stiff upper backs cause rounded posture, shoulder pain and low back pain, and limit the golf swing. Daily T spine drills fix it.
Cue 1: Keep the hips still (knee pinned or in quadruped)
Cue 2: Rotate/extend through the upper back, follow the hand with the eyes
Cue 3: Breathe out into the end range
Common faults: Rotating from the low back; Rushing; Forcing range
Progress to: Bear Crawl (G2); Quadruped Thoracic Rotation (G2); Spiderman Lunge with Rotation (G2)
Progress by: Add a reach, hold end range longer
Regress by: Smaller range, seated version
Same level swaps: Thread the Needle; Open Book Stretch; Open Book (Side Lying)
Joint notes: Very safe. Osteoporosis: avoid forced flexion; gentle rotation and extension are fine.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down

Pattern: Single leg: knee over toes step (VMO)
Why: Ben Patrick's entry level knee builder from ATG Zero: standing on a low step on the ball of the foot, the knee travels forward over the toes as the other heel lowers to tap the floor. It teaches the quads, not the joint, to own the knees over toes position and is the first step towards the ATG split squat.
Cue 1: Stand on a low step, working heel raised on a small plate or wedge (Poliquin) or on the toes (Patrick)
Cue 2: Slowly lower the other heel towards the floor by bending the working knee forward over the toes
Cue 3: Lightly tap and drive back up through the front of the foot, keeping the knee in line
Common faults: Hips shifting back instead of the knee travelling forward; Knee caving inward; Dropping fast instead of controlling the lowering
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); Split Squat (DB) (G2)
Progress by: Higher step, slower tempo, hold DBs, progress to step downs and front foot elevated split squats
Regress by: Lower step, hand on the rig, partial range
Same level swaps: Poliquin Step Up; Petersen Step Up
Joint notes: Knee friendly when kept pain free. Start with a very low step (5 to 10cm) and hand support. Ideal in every knee pain programme.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 20 each leg, slow lowering (3s)

Why: Ben Patrick's signature exercise: a long split squat where the front knee travels well past the toes with the heel staying down and the back knee lowers to the floor, giving a deep hip flexor stretch on the back leg. It builds strength in the deepest knee position and hip flexor flexibility at the same time. Start with the front foot elevated and hand support, hold the bottom for time (e.g. 30s), then add reps and load.
Cue 1: Long split stance, both feet pointing forward, hip width apart
Cue 2: Lower the back knee straight down towards the floor
Cue 3: Push through the front foot to stand, keep the torso tall
Common faults: Stance too narrow (tightrope), losing balance; Front heel lifting; Lunging forward instead of dropping down
Progress to: Barbell Split Squat (G3); Band Resisted Split Squat (G3); Offset Single Arm Split Squat (G3)
Progress by: Add load, elevate the front foot (ATG style), then elevate the back foot (RFESS)
Regress to: Split Squat (Supported) (G1); Split Squat (Bodyweight) (G1); TRX Assisted Split Squat (G1)
Regress by: TRX or rig assisted split squat, shorter range, isometric split squat hold
Same level swaps: SSB Split Squat; Split Squat (DB); Cable Split Squat
Joint notes: Knee friendly when depth is controlled. Use a pad under the back knee. Hold a support for balance in seniors.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)
Coach sources: Boyle, Squat University, Ben Patrick (front foot elevated)

Joint notes: Knee friendly when depth is controlled. Use a pad under the back knee. Hold a support for balance in seniors.

Coach sources: Boyle, Squat University, Ben Patrick (front foot elevated)

Muscles: Quads (rectus femoris in a lengthened position), hip flexors
Why: Kneeling, the body leans back as one line from knee to head, lengthening and strengthening the quads (especially rectus femoris) through a range most people never train. Ben Patrick uses it for knee resilience and hip flexor length. Use a band or partner for assistance and short range first.
Variation notes: Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress).
Cue 1: Hold a post or TRX for support
Cue 2: Rise onto the toes, push the knees forward and lean the body back as one straight line from knee to shoulder
Cue 3: Lower only as far as pain free, drive back up through the quads
Common faults: Bending at the hips (turns it into a normal squat); Dropping too deep too early; Letting go of the support before ready
Progress to: SSB Squat (G3); SSB Box Squat (G3); Nordic Curl (Full) (G3)
Progress by: Increase range, reduce hand assistance, add a plate at the chest, progress towards reverse Nordic
Regress to: Patrick Step (G1); Elephant Walk (G1); KOT Calf Raise (G1)
Regress by: Short range only, more hand support, swap to Spanish squat or heels elevated goblet squat
Same level swaps: Sissy Squat (Assisted); Sissy Squat (Assisted, Short Range)
Joint notes: Earn it. Start short range with hand support. Avoid with acute knee pain, recent knee surgery or knee replacements unless cleared.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 6 to 12 reps, slow lowering, hand support

Muscles: Calves (gastrocnemius straight knee, soleus bent knee), Achilles
Why: Knees over toes calf raise (Ben Patrick): the knee is pushed forward over the toes during the raise, training the calf and Achilles in the bent knee position used in walking downhill, stairs and squatting.
Cue 1: Full stretch at the bottom
Cue 2: Rise to the highest point on the big toe
Cue 3: Pause, lower slowly (3s)
Common faults: Bouncing; Rolling to the outside of the foot; Partial range
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)
Progress by: Single leg, off a step, add load
Regress by: Two legs, hand support, flat floor
Same level swaps: Single Leg Calf Raise; Calf Raise (Straight Knee); Seated Calf Raise (Bent Knee)
Joint notes: Achilles pain: slow heavy calf raises are rehab gold.
Default prescription: 3 x 12 to 20 (slow)

Why: Loaded tibialis raise using a tib bar or a plate/KB over the feet while seated. Ben Patrick's advanced standard is around 25% bodyweight for 5 x 5. Strong shins protect the knees and ankles and balance the calves.
Cue 1: Back against a wall, heels 30 to 50cm away
Cue 2: Lift the toes up as high as possible
Cue 3: Lower slowly
Common faults: Bending the knees; Rushing; Partial range
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)
Progress by: Feet further from the wall, single leg, tib bar load
Regress by: Closer to the wall
Same level swaps: Tibialis Raise
Joint notes: Universally safe.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 x 20 to 25

Muscles: Quads, glutes, adductors, upper back, core
Why: Squatting with the heels on a slant board lets the knees travel well forward with the torso upright, loading the quads and VMO with less ankle demand. A Ben Patrick and Squat University tool for knee health and quad strength.
Cue 1: Hold the bell tight to the chest, elbows pointing down
Cue 2: Push the knees out and sit between the hips, chest proud
Cue 3: Drive up through the whole foot, squeeze the glutes at the top
Common faults: Rounding the upper back and letting the weight pull you forward; Heels lifting; Knees caving inward on the way up
Progress to: Paused Goblet Squat (G3); 1.5 Rep Goblet Squat (G3)
Progress by: Add load, tempo (4-1-1-0), pause at the bottom, 1.5 reps, move to double KB front squat or SSB squat
Regress to: Goblet Box Squat (G1); Box Squat (G1); TRX Assisted Squat (G1)
Regress by: Goblet squat to a box, TRX assisted squat, lighter bell
Same level swaps: Goblet Squat (KB); Goblet Squat (DB); Tempo Goblet Squat
Joint notes: Knee and back friendly. Heels elevated version helps stiff ankles. Use a box for depth control with knee pain. Upper back can fatigue first as loads get heavy.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
Coach sources: Dan John, Squat University, Cosgrove, Boyle

Why: The safety squat bar lets members back squat heavy without needing shoulder mobility to hold a straight bar, and its forward pitch keeps the torso upright. It is Optimal's main heavy squat tool for 40+ members with cranky shoulders, elbows or wrists. DeFranco built his reputation using it.

Cue 2: Push knees out over the middle of the foot, sit between the hips
Cue 3: Drive up with the chest leading, don't let the bar tip you forward
Common faults: Letting the bar pull the chest forward and rounding the upper back; Losing the brace at the bottom; Cutting depth as the weight goes up
Progress to: SSB Pause Squat (G4); Anderson Squat (G4); Tempo Back Squat (G4)
Progress by: Add load (double progression), pause squats, tempo 4-1-X-0, SSB split squats, rep maxes on rotating variations (Teams G4)
Regress to: Barbell Box Squat (G2); Banded Barbell Box Squat (G2)
Regress by: SSB box squat to a higher box, goblet squat, front loaded DB squat
Same level swaps: SSB Box Squat; Zercher Squat; DB Front Squat
Joint notes: Shoulder and wrist friendly. Still a spinal load: check back history. For knee pain use a box to control depth.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8

Why: Reverse lunge loaded with the safety squat bar for heavy single leg strength without grip or shoulder limitations.
Variation notes: Safety squat bar: heavy loading without needing shoulder mobility to hold a straight bar; DeFranco's go to for cranky shoulders.
Cue 1: Stand tall, step one foot back
Cue 2: Drop the back knee towards the floor, front shin fairly vertical
Cue 3: Drive through the front heel to stand back up
Common faults: Stepping too short; Front knee collapsing; Leaning forward and rounding
Progress to: Slider Reverse Lunge (G3); Deficit Reverse Lunge (G3); Barbell Reverse Lunge (G3)
Progress by: Add load, deficit (front foot on a plate), knee drive at the top, barbell/landmine
Regress to: Split Squat (Supported) (G1); Split Squat (Bodyweight) (G1); TRX Assisted Split Squat (G1)
Regress by: Split squat (static), hand support, shorter range
Same level swaps: Reverse Lunge (DB); Cable Reverse Lunge; Goblet Reverse Lunge
Joint notes: Most knee friendly lunge. Use a pad and hand support for beginners.
Default prescription: 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)

Why: Good morning with the safety squat bar: the handles and padding make it more comfortable and safer to learn than a straight bar good morning. Builds hamstrings and back extensors. Teams G3 to G4 only and not for low back pain.
Variation notes: Safety squat bar: heavy loading without needing shoulder mobility to hold a straight bar; DeFranco's go to for cranky shoulders.
Cue 1: Soft knees, brace, push the hips back
Cue 2: Keep the spine long and neutral
Cue 3: Stand up by driving the hips forward
Common faults: Rounding the spine; Bending the knees too much; Going deeper than hamstring length allows
Progress to: Barbell Good Morning (G3); Barbell Romanian Deadlift (G3); Paused DB RDL (G3)
Progress by: Band → light barbell → SSB good morning, tempo, pause
Regress to: Bodyweight Good Morning (G1); Hip Hinge to Wall (G1); Hip Hinge Dowel Drill (G1)
Regress by: Bodyweight, dowel hinge drill
Same level swaps: Seated Good Morning; Banded Good Morning; Single Leg Good Morning
Joint notes: Loaded good mornings are not for low back pain. Keep loads light and range controlled for 40+.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9

Why: Vern Gambetta's multi directional lunge sequence: a lunge forward, to the side, rotational (turning 135 degrees) and backward on each leg. It warms up the hips in all three planes and builds balance and multi plane strength. Ideal warm up for golf and 40+ hips.
Cue 1: Move through big comfortable ranges
Cue 2: Increase range each rep
Cue 3: Breathe and stay controlled
Common faults: Rushing; Bouncing into range; Skipping the warm up
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)
Progress by: Bigger range, add reaches
Regress by: Smaller range, hand support
Same level swaps: A March; Inchworm; Crab Reach
Joint notes: Safe for almost everyone.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 x 5 to 10 each side (or 20 to 30m)

Why: Joe DeFranco's 10 to 15 minute lower body mobility routine: foam roll IT band and adductors, lacrosse ball glutes, bent knee iron cross, roll overs into V sits, rocking frog stretch, fire hydrant circles, slow mountain climbers, Cossack squats, seated piriformis stretch, rear foot elevated hip flexor stretch. Optimal uses a shortened 5 to 6 drill version before lower body sessions.
Cue 1: Move through big comfortable ranges
Cue 2: Increase range each rep
Cue 3: Breathe and stay controlled
Common faults: Rushing; Bouncing into range; Skipping the warm up
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)
Progress by: Bigger range, add reaches
Regress by: Smaller range, hand support
Same level swaps: A March; Inchworm; Crab Reach
Joint notes: Safe for almost everyone.
Default prescription: 1 to 2 x 5 to 10 each side (or 20 to 30m)

Why: Joe DeFranco's quick upper body mobility routine for shoulders and thoracic spine (band pass throughs, wall slides, scapular and T spine drills, lat and pec stretches). Use before pressing and pulling days.
Cue 1: Move through big comfortable ranges
Cue 2: Increase range each rep
Cue 3: Breathe and stay controlled
Common faults: Rushing; Bouncing into range; Skipping the warm up
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)
Progress by: Bigger range, add reaches
Regress by: Smaller range, hand support
Same level swaps: A March; Inchworm; Crab Reach
Joint notes: Safe for almost everyone.

Exercise: McGill Big 3 (Curl Up, Side Plank, Bird Dog)
Why: Professor Stuart McGill's daily core routine for back health: modified curl up, side plank and bird dog, each held 8 to 10 seconds in a descending pyramid (e.g. 6, 4, 2 reps). Builds core endurance and stiffness without stressing the discs. Default warm up for any member with back history.
Cue 1: Lie on your back, one knee bent, hands under the low back
Cue 2: Brace and lift the head and shoulders slightly as one unit
Cue 3: Hold 8 to 10s, lower
Common faults: Tucking the chin; Flattening the low back; Curling up too high
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)
Progress by: Raise elbows off the floor, longer holds
Regress by: Shorter holds
Same level swaps: McGill Curl Up
Joint notes: Back pain friendly. Part of the Big 3.
Default prescription: Descending pyramid: 6, 4, 2 reps with 8 to 10s holds

Why: Paul Chek's inner unit drill: on hands and knees, let the belly relax then draw the belly button gently towards the spine without moving the spine, hold and breathe. Teaches deep core activation before loading (stabilisers before prime movers).
Cue 1: Lie in position, hands on the lower ribs
Cue 2: Breathe in through the nose expanding 360 degrees (belly, sides, back)
Cue 3: Exhale slowly fully, feeling the ribs drop
Common faults: Chest and shoulder breathing; Arching the back; Rushing
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)
Progress by: Add movement (dead bug with breathing)
Regress by: Shorter sets
Same level swaps: Pelvic Tilt; 90/90 Breathing; Pelvic Tilt (Supine)
Joint notes: Universally safe. Great on RED readiness days.
Default prescription: 5 to 10 slow breaths

Why: Paul Chek's postural endurance exercise: lying face down, lift the chest slightly and rotate the thumbs out to squeeze the shoulder blades, hold. Strengthens the upper back and spinal extensors that hold upright posture.
Cue 1: Hinge at the hips, keep the spine long
Cue 2: Lift to a straight line from head to heels using the glutes
Cue 3: Lower with control
Common faults: Hyperextending at the top; Swinging/using momentum; Rounding heavily at the bottom under load
Progress to: SSB Squat (G3); SSB Box Squat (G3); Nordic Curl (Full) (G3)
Progress by: Hold a plate, single leg, pause at the top
Regress to: Reverse Hyper (Bench, Light) (G1); 45 Degree Back Extension (Bodyweight) (G1)
Regress by: Superman, bird dog, shorter range
Same level swaps: Reverse Hyper (Bench); Superman (Alternating); 45 Degree Back Extension
Joint notes: Good for most back pain when kept to neutral. Avoid loaded flexion at the bottom for osteoporosis.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
Coach sources: DeFranco (reverse hyper), McGill, Paul Chek (prone cobra)

Exercise: Swiss Ball Supine Lateral Ball Roll (Chek)
Why: Paul Chek's twist pattern exercise: lying with the shoulders on a Swiss ball and hips up, arms out holding a light weight, shuffle sideways across the ball keeping the body level. Trains rotational stability of the trunk and hips.
Variation notes: Swiss ball adds instability for core control (Paul Chek); keep loads modest.
Cue 1: Arms long, pivot the back foot
Cue 2: Turn from the hips and upper back together
Cue 3: Control the return through the middle
Common faults: Rotating only at the low back; Arms bending; Moving too fast
Progress to: SSB Squat (G3); SSB Box Squat (G3); Nordic Curl (Full) (G3)
Progress by: Heavier, faster, split stance
Regress to: Patrick Step (G1); Elephant Walk (G1); KOT Calf Raise (G1)
Regress by: Lighter, smaller range, anti rotation instead
Same level swaps: Landmine 180; Landmine Rainbow; Landmine Rotation
Joint notes: Avoid fast loaded rotation with acute back pain.
Default prescription: 2 to 3 sets x 6 to 10 reps each side (or 20 to 40s), slow and controlled

Pattern: Total body: Turkish get up / windmill
Muscles: Shoulder stability, core, hips, whole body
Why: Getting down to the floor and back up with as little support as possible. A key longevity skill (Attia, Dan John) and part of the Optimal screen. Progress from using a chair to hands only to no hands.
Cue 1: Eyes on the bell, arm locked
Cue 2: Move through each step slowly: roll to elbow, hand, high bridge, sweep the leg, kneel, stand
Cue 3: Reverse every step with control
Common faults: Rushing; Bent arm; Losing sight of the bell
Progress to: SSB Squat (G3); SSB Box Squat (G3); Nordic Curl (Full) (G3)
Progress by: Heavier bell, full get up
Regress to: Half Turkish Get Up (G1); Turkish Get Up (Light) (G1)
Regress by: Half get up, shoe on the fist, no weight
Same level swaps: KB Windmill; Arm Bar (KB); Turkish Get Up
Joint notes: Learn with a shoe or no weight first. Shoulder pain: half get up with no load only.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 reps each side, slow
Coach sources: Dan John, Pavel Tsatsouline, Gray Cook

Pattern: Total body: Turkish get up / windmill
Muscles: Shoulder stability, core, hips, whole body
Why: From half kneeling, stand up without using the hands (then lower back down). Builds the strength and balance needed to get off the floor, and is a stepping stone to the Turkish get up.
Variation notes: Kneeling position locks the hips so the core has to control the trunk and stops the legs cheating.
Cue 1: Eyes on the bell, arm locked
Cue 2: Move through each step slowly: roll to elbow, hand, high bridge, sweep the leg, kneel, stand
Cue 3: Reverse every step with control
Common faults: Rushing; Bent arm; Losing sight of the bell
Progress to: SSB Squat (G3); SSB Box Squat (G3); Nordic Curl (Full) (G3)
Progress by: Heavier bell, full get up
Regress to: Half Turkish Get Up (G1); Turkish Get Up (Light) (G1)
Regress by: Half get up, shoe on the fist, no weight
Same level swaps: KB Windmill; Arm Bar (KB); Turkish Get Up
Joint notes: Learn with a shoe or no weight first. Shoulder pain: half get up with no load only.
Default prescription: 3 to 5 reps each side, slow
Coach sources: Dan John, Pavel Tsatsouline, Gray Cook

Why: Stand up from a chair as fast as possible, sit down slowly. Trains power, which declines faster than strength with age, using the safest possible movement. Seniors programme staple.
Variation notes: Fast/power version: move with intent, stop when speed drops.
Cue 1: Sit tall on a box or chair, feet slightly back under the knees
Cue 2: Lean the chest forward, push the floor away and stand up tall
Cue 3: Sit back down slowly with control, don't flop
Common faults: Using the hands to push off; Feet too far forward; Collapsing back down onto the seat
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)
Progress by: Lower the box, hold a weight at the chest, stand up as fast as possible (power), single leg sit to stand
Regress by: Raise the seat, use hands on thighs or a TRX for help, reduce reps
Same level swaps: Sit to Stand (Chair); Squat to Box Stand Up (Bodyweight)
Joint notes: Suitable for almost everyone. Raise the seat height for painful knees or hips. Single leg version needs good knee control.
Default prescription: 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps (or max reps in 30s for testing), stand up fast, lower slowly
Coach sources: Seniors research (functional testing), Gambetta (fundamental movement), Attia (centenarian decathlon)

Muscles: Foot, ankle, hip stabilisers, nervous system
Why: Standing heel to toe (one foot directly in front of the other) near a support. A falls prevention staple and seniors programme warm up.
Cue 1: Stand tall near a support
Cue 2: Grip the floor with the foot, soft knee
Cue 3: Hold or reach while keeping the hips level
Common faults: Locking the knee; Holding the breath; Doing it far from support
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)
Progress by: Eyes closed, cushion, reach, catch a ball
Regress by: Hand on support, tandem stance
Same level swaps: Heel to Toe Walk; Single Leg Balance; Star Excursion Balance
Joint notes: Always near a rail or rig for seniors.
Default prescription: 3 x 20 to 30s each leg

Muscles: Foot, ankle, hip stabilisers, nervous system
Why: Walking in a straight line placing the heel directly in front of the toes. Trains dynamic balance and gait (Gambetta: postural alignment and dynamic balance are the foundation).
Cue 1: Stand tall near a support
Cue 2: Grip the floor with the foot, soft knee
Cue 3: Hold or reach while keeping the hips level
Common faults: Locking the knee; Holding the breath; Doing it far from support
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)

Regress by: Hand on support, tandem stance
Same level swaps: Single Leg Balance; Tandem Stance Balance; Star Excursion Balance
Joint notes: Always near a rail or rig for seniors.
Default prescription: 3 x 20 to 30s each leg

Muscles: Foot, ankle, hip stabilisers, nervous system
Why: Standing on one leg and reaching the other foot to points on an imaginary clock. Builds balance, ankle and hip control.
Cue 1: Stand tall near a support
Cue 2: Grip the floor with the foot, soft knee
Cue 3: Hold or reach while keeping the hips level
Common faults: Locking the knee; Holding the breath; Doing it far from support
Progress to: ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); SSB Good Morning (G2)
